mockTask.q: A detector flags 5% of benign traffic and catches 99% of attacks. Attacks are 1% of traffic. Roughly what fraction of flags are real attacks?
mockTask.explain: Bayes with base rates: only ~17% of flags are real — the base-rate effect.

notes.title: Describing data, computed
notes.body: Worked example on latency samples (ms): [12, 15, 18, 22, 22, 27, 31, 35, 40, 48]. Mean = Σx/n = 270/10 = **27**. Median (middle value) = **24.5**. Population std dev = **10.91**. Mean − median gap signals skew: the 48 drags the mean above the median. Rule: report center AND spread together; a mean without a spread is half a fact. The analyst and data-science modules assume this entire module.

notes.title: Probability rules
notes.body: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B|A); for independent events, P(A)·P(B). P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A and B). Worked example: two independent deploys each fail with p=0.1. P(both fail) = 0.1×0.1 = **0.010000000000000002**. P(at least one fails) = 1 − P(neither) = 1 − 0.9² = **0.19**. Complement-first ('1 minus the boring case') solves most 'at least one' problems. Independence is an assumption to check, not a default: correlated failures break the multiplication.

notes.title: Conditional probability and Bayes
notes.body: Bayes: P(D|+) = P(+|D)·P(D) / P(+). Worked example: 1% of requests are malicious (0.01); the detector catches 99% of malicious and flags 5% of benign. P(+) = 0.99×0.01 + 0.05×0.99 = **0.0594**. So P(malicious | flagged) = 0.0099/0.0594 = **0.167** — only about 1 in 6 flags is real. This is the base-rate effect: with rare events, even good tests produce mostly false positives. Every alert-fatigue argument in operations is Bayes in disguise.

notes.title: Expectation
notes.body: E[X] = Σ x·P(x): the long-run average. Worked example: a retry policy succeeds on attempt 1 with p=0.7, attempt 2 with p=0.2, attempt 3 with p=0.1 (then gives up). Expected attempts = 1×0.7 + 2×0.2 + 3×0.1 = **1.4000000000000001**. Linearity of expectation: E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even when X,Y are dependent — the workhorse for analyzing total cost, total latency, total errors across components without modeling their joint distribution.

notes.title: The binomial distribution, computed
notes.body: P(X=k) = C(n,k)·p^k·(1−p)^(n−k). Worked example: 10 requests, each fails independently with p=0.5 (a coin). P(exactly 3 fail) = C(10,3)×0.5^3×0.5^7 = 120×0.5^10 = **0.1172**. Sanity: probabilities over k=0..10 sum to 1.000000 = 1 ✓. Use the binomial for 'k of n independent trials' questions — canary failures, bit errors, A/B conversions.

notes.title: Percentiles and SLO math
notes.body: Worked on response times (ms): [22, 25, 28, 31, 33, 35, 38, 41, 45, 52, 61, 78, 120, 210, 400]. Sorted already. p50 (median) = **41** ms; p99 = **373.4** ms. The mean would be polluted by the 400 ms outlier; percentiles describe what users actually feel. SLO connection: a '99.9% of requests < 300 ms' objective is a percentile statement — an error budget of 0.1% means 0.015 bad requests allowed per 15 in this sample's scale. Measure percentiles on real data, never assume normality for latency.

notes.title: Vectors and the dot product
notes.body: Worked example: u=[1, 2, 3], v=[4, -1, 2]. Dot product u·v = 1×4 + 2×(−1) + 3×2 = 4 − 2 + 6 = **8**. Norm ||u|| = √(1+4+9) = √14 ≈ **3.7417**. Cosine similarity = u·v/(||u||·||v||) = 8/(√14×√21) ≈ **0.4666**. Dot products measure alignment: positive = similar direction, zero = orthogonal, negative = opposing. Embeddings, search ranking, and attention scores are all dot products at scale.

notes.title: Solving linear systems
notes.body: Worked example: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2. Add the equations: 3x = 9, so x = **3**; then y = 7 − 2×3 = **1**. Check: 2×3+1 = 7 ✓; 3−1 = 2 ✓. Elimination is the algorithm; the geometry is two lines intersecting at one point. A system has a unique solution exactly when the coefficient matrix is invertible (nonzero determinant).

notes.title: Determinant and invertibility
notes.body: For 2×2 [[a,b],[c,d]], det = ad − bc. Worked: A=[[1, 2], [3, 4]], det = 1×4 − 2×3 = **-2**. Nonzero → invertible → the system Ax=b has exactly one solution. det = 0 means the rows are dependent: the map crushes a dimension (area → 0). |det| is the area-scaling factor of the transformation. Singular matrices (det 0) are why 'matrix is singular' errors appear — the inverse doesn't exist.

notes.title: Eigenvalues of a 2×2, computed
notes.body: Eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0. For A=[[1, 2], [3, 4]]: (1−λ)(4−λ) − 6 = λ² − 5λ + (-2) ... precisely λ² − (trace)λ + det = 0, i.e. λ² − 5λ + -2 = 0. Discriminant 5² − 4×-2 = **33**. λ = (5 ± √33)/2 = **5.3723**, **-0.3723**. Check: λ₁+λ₂ = 5.0000 = trace ✓; λ₁×λ₂ = -2.0000 = det ✓. Eigenvalues are the scaling factors along the matrix's natural axes — the basis of PCA and stability analysis.

notes.title: Least squares in miniature
notes.body: Fit y = mx through points (1,2), (2,3), (3,5): minimize Σ(mxᵢ − yᵢ)². Normal equation: m = Σxᵢyᵢ/Σxᵢ². Σxᵢyᵢ = 1×2+2×3+3×5 = **23**; Σxᵢ² = 1+4+9 = **14**; m = 23/14 ≈ **1.6429**. Residuals: predictions 1.64, 3.29, 4.93 vs actual 2, 3, 5 — the best single slope in the least-squares sense. This is linear regression with one parameter; the full version solves (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. ML modules represent data as vectors and matrices.

cards.front: How do you explain window functions in a SQL interview?
cards.back: ‘Calculations across rows without collapsing them’: ROW_NUMBER/RANK for top-N per group, LAG/LEAD for period-over-period, running totals with ordered frames. The key contrast: GROUP BY collapses rows; windows keep row detail and add context.

cards.front: When do you reach for a CTE?
cards.back: Multi-step logic that reads top-to-bottom: each CTE is a named pipeline stage, chained like transforms. More readable than nested subqueries, and recursive CTEs (anchor + UNION ALL) handle hierarchies and date spines. The interview line: ‘CTEs are how I show my work.’

cards.front: How do you find ‘what’s missing’ in SQL?
cards.back: The anti-join: LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.key IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS (preferred — NULL-safe, unlike NOT IN). ‘Customers with no orders,’ ‘products never sold’ — this pattern is an interview staple.

cards.front: What does ‘aggregation at the right grain’ mean?
cards.back: GROUP BY must match the question’s unit: revenue per day vs per customer are different queries with different answers. State the grain explicitly (‘one row per customer-month’) before writing the query — interviewers score this discipline.

cards.front: How do you do set operations and conditional aggregation in SQL?
cards.back: UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT for set logic (UNION ALL when dupes are fine — faster, no dedup pass). Conditional aggregation — SUM(CASE WHEN …) — pivots and computes segment metrics in one pass. The interview line: ‘one scan, many answers.’

cards.front: What's the interview line for logical query order?
cards.back: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → window functions → ORDER BY: 'I write in SELECT order but think in execution order.' It explains why aliases aren't visible in WHERE and why windows can't be filtered in the same level.

cards.front: How do you talk about query performance in a SQL interview?
cards.back: Start with EXPLAIN: show you read the plan, not the query. Name the three big costs — sequential scans on large filtered tables, sorts that spill to disk, and nested loops on big inputs — and the matching fixes: indexes for selective filters, CLUSTER or covering indexes for sorted access, and join-order awareness. The interview line: 'I make the database prove it with EXPLAIN before I rewrite anything.'

cards.front: What's the interview line for self-joins?
cards.back: Reach for a self-join when a row must be compared against other rows of the same table — consecutive events, pairs, or 'find what changed'. Alias the table twice (a and b), join on the key plus the ordering condition (b.ts > a.ts), and filter for the nearest match. The honest line: 'Any question with the word consecutive or previous is probably a self-join, so I alias the table twice.'

cards.front: Putting a filter on an aggregated value in WHERE instead of HAVING is wrong because:
cards.back: **WHERE runs before aggregation — aggregate filters belong in HAVING** — Logical query order: WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY aggregates, HAVING filters groups. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: A sequential scan in EXPLAIN is a red flag when:
cards.back: **It’s on a large table with a selective filter — a missing or unused index** — Full scans are fine for small tables; on large filtered tables they signal missing index support. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: UNION ALL vs UNION differ in that:
cards.back: **UNION ALL keeps duplicates and skips the dedup sort — faster when dupes are fine** — UNION’s implicit DISTINCT costs a sort; ALL avoids it when duplicates don’t matter. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) vs COUNT(*) differ when:
cards.back: **Rows aren’t unique per customer — COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(DISTINCT) counts customers** — Grain discipline: know what one row represents before choosing the aggregate. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **window function** — A calculation across rows related to the current row — ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG/LEAD, running totals — computed without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY does.
- **ROW_NUMBER** — Assigns a unique sequential integer within each partition in the specified order; the tool for top-N-per-group when paired with a CTE and an outer filter.
- **RANK / DENSE_RANK** — Rankings that honor ties: RANK leaves gaps after ties, DENSE_RANK does not; use either when equal values must share a rank.
- **LAG / LEAD** — Reads the previous or next row's value inside an ordered partition; the workhorse for period-over-period deltas without a self-join.
- **frame clause** — ROWS or RANGE bounds on a window (e.g. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) defining which rows the function sees; without ORDER BY the frame has no meaning.
- **CTE (common table expression)** — A named temporary result set (WITH ...) that structures a query into readable top-to-bottom stages; chained CTEs read like a pipeline.
- **recursive CTE** — A CTE with an anchor query plus a UNION ALL recursive term; the way to walk hierarchies and generate date spines.
- **semi-join** — An existence filter ('has at least one': EXISTS or IN) that never fans out rows; the safe answer to yes/no membership questions.
- **anti-join** — A 'has none' filter: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS (NULL-safe, unlike NOT IN); the pattern for 'what is missing' questions.
- **grain** — The unit one row represents (per customer, per day, per customer-month); GROUP BY must match the question's grain or the aggregate answers a different question.
- **HAVING** — Filters groups after aggregation; WHERE filters rows before it — an aggregate filter in WHERE is always wrong.
- **UNION vs UNION ALL** — UNION dedupes (implicit DISTINCT, costs a sort); UNION ALL keeps duplicates and skips the pass — faster when duplicates don't matter.
- **conditional aggregation** — SUM(CASE WHEN ...) patterns that compute segment metrics in one scan: 'one scan, many answers.'
- **query plan (EXPLAIN)** — The database's execution strategy; a sequential scan on a large filtered table signals a missing or unused index.

Sources for this module:
- **PostgreSQL Documentation** (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/) — The SQL reference this spine drills against: window functions, CTEs, recursion, and query planning.
- **Mode SQL Tutorial** (https://mode.com/sql-tutorial/) — Free interactive SQL tutorial, from basic selects through window functions and analytics patterns.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
The SQL layer interviewers actually probe: not syntax trivia, but choosing the right construct for the grain of the question — and explaining why the query is fast or slow.

The drill loop for this module: one pattern at a time, timed, narrated aloud. Each rep follows the same steps so the method — not the query — becomes the habit you carry into the interview.
1. State the grain out loud before writing anything: 'one row per customer-month.' Write it as a comment at the top of the query.
2. Sketch the CTE stages on paper or in the editor: clean -> enrich -> aggregate -> rank. Name each stage; never nest subqueries three deep when a CTE would show the work.
3. Write the core logic first (joins and grain), then layer on window functions in an outer CTE — window functions cannot appear in WHERE, so plan the two-step from the start.
4. Run the query against a tiny mental dataset (three rows per table) and trace each stage's output by hand; fix grain and join-type mistakes here, not after.
5. Read the EXPLAIN output: look for sequential scans on large filtered tables, and confirm join order and index use. Be ready to say why the query is fast or slow.
6. Re-do the same problem with a different construct (self-join vs LAG, subquery vs CTE) and name the tradeoff aloud — interviewers probe the choice, not just the answer.

-- Top-N per group: the canonical window-function pattern
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         order_date,
         amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                          ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;  -- latest 3 orders per customer

-- Anti-join: customers with no orders (NULL-safe)
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);

notes.title: Worked example: Putting a filter on an aggregated value in WHERE instead of HAVING is…
notes.body:
**Problem.** Putting a filter on an aggregated value in WHERE instead of HAVING is wrong because:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** WHERE runs before aggregation — aggregate filters belong in HAVING
- **Why:** Logical query order: WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY aggregates, HAVING filters groups. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Logical query order: WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY aggregates, HAVING filters groups.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Data interviews test judgment as much as syntax. In Advanced SQL for Data Engineers, these habits fail candidates:
- **SQL without thinking in sets.** Row-by-row mental models break on real queries. Think in sets, joins, and aggregations — say the grain of every result out loud.
- **No business framing.** A metric without a decision it informs is trivia. Every analysis in Advanced SQL for Data Engineers starts from: what decision does this change?
- **Experiment sloppiness.** Peeking at results, ignoring power, confusing correlation with lift. Design the test before you look at the data.
- **Pretty charts, no insight.** Visualization is argument, not decoration. Every chart needs a title that states the conclusion, not the topic.
- **Can't walk the pipeline end to end.** Knowing the modeling step but not ingestion, validation, or serving. Interviewers probe the seams — own the whole pipeline.
- **Answering before clarifying.** Ambiguous question, instant query. Ask about grain, time window, definitions, and edge cases first — it mirrors the real job.

quiz.q: Putting a filter on an aggregated value in WHERE instead of HAVING is wrong because:
choices: WHERE runs before aggregation — aggregate filters belong in HAVING
quiz.explain: Logical query order: WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY aggregates, HAVING filters groups. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: A sequential scan in EXPLAIN is a red flag when:
choices: It’s on a large table with a selective filter — a missing or unused index
quiz.explain: Full scans are fine for small tables; on large filtered tables they signal missing index support. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: UNION ALL vs UNION differ in that:
choices: UNION ALL keeps duplicates and skips the dedup sort — faster when dupes are fine
quiz.explain: UNION’s implicit DISTINCT costs a sort; ALL avoids it when duplicates don’t matter. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) vs COUNT(*) differ when:
choices: Rows aren’t unique per customer — COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(DISTINCT) counts customers
quiz.explain: Grain discipline: know what one row represents before choosing the aggregate. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: Which ranking function leaves gaps after ties?
quiz.explain: RANK assigns the same rank to ties and skips the next numbers; DENSE_RANK doesn't skip. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: To compute each order's running total per customer, you write:
choices: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
quiz.explain: The partition keeps per-customer scope, the order plus frame accumulates correctly. See the 'Hands-on procedure' drill steps in this module.

quiz.q: NOT IN on a nullable subquery column is unsafe because:
choices: Any NULL makes the predicate UNKNOWN, returning zero rows
quiz.explain: Three-valued logic: NOT IN with a NULL never evaluates true. Use NOT EXISTS. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: A recursive CTE requires which two parts?
choices: An anchor query plus a UNION ALL recursive term
A frame clause and a partition
quiz.explain: Anchor seeds the rows; the recursive term extends them until no new rows appear. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: Why does the top-N-per-group pattern need a CTE (or subquery)?
choices: Window functions evaluate after WHERE, so you can't filter on the row number in the same query level
quiz.explain: Logical query order puts windows after WHERE — filter one level out. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'west' THEN revenue END) is an example of:
choices: Conditional aggregation — one scan producing segment metrics
quiz.explain: 'One scan, many answers': the CASE filters inside the aggregate instead of rescanning. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

cards.front: What pandas patterns must be muscle memory?
cards.back: groupby-agg-transform (split-apply-combine), merges with validated cardinality, pivots/melt for reshaping, and vectorized ops instead of row loops. The interview line: ‘I think in whole-DataFrame operations.’

cards.front: How do you handle files too big for memory in pandas?
cards.back: Chunked reading (chunksize) with incremental aggregation, dtype downcasting, reading only needed columns (usecols), or switching to a lazy engine (Polars/Dask/Spark). The interview line: ‘I never assume the data fits.’

cards.front: Why do datetimes and timezones cause interview bugs?
cards.back: Naive vs aware mixing, DST transitions (nonexistent/ambiguous times), and storing local time instead of UTC. The interview line: ‘store UTC, convert at display — and never do arithmetic on naive datetimes.’

cards.front: How do you handle nulls, duplicates, and type coercion?
cards.back: Profile first (missingness patterns, dup counts), decide per column (drop/impute/flag — never silently), dedupe on defined keys, and coerce types explicitly with errors='raise' thinking. The interview line: ‘every cleaning decision gets a reason, out loud.’

cards.front: Why do interviewers demand vectorized pandas?
cards.back: Row loops (iterrows) are Python-speed; vectorized ops run in C: groupby-transform, boolean masks, np.where, string methods. The performance gap is 10–100x — and the code is shorter. ‘No Python loops over rows’ is the rule.

cards.front: What's the interview line for chunked reading?
cards.back: 'I never assume the data fits': chunksize with incremental aggregation, usecols to read only what's needed, dtype downcasting — and if the frame still won't fit, a lazy engine. Memory discipline is a design decision, not an afterthought.

cards.front: When do you reach for Parquet instead of CSV in a pipeline?
cards.back: CSV is human-readable and universal; Parquet is columnar, compressed, typed, and partitionable. In an interview: choose Parquet the moment a human isn't reading the file — it's 5-10x smaller and lets Spark/presto read only needed columns. The interview line: 'CSV for handoffs to humans, Parquet for everything a machine reads twice.'

cards.front: How do you discuss testing data transforms in an interview?
cards.back: Three levels: row-level unit tests on small hand-built frames (pandas.testing or plain asserts), property checks on output (row counts, key uniqueness, no nulls in required fields), and golden-file tests on sampled real data. The line: 'If a transform can't be tested on a 10-row fixture, I don't trust it on 10 million rows.'

cards.front: Pure transform functions are testable because:
cards.back: **Determinism: no mocks needed, every case is an input/output pair** — Purity removes the test setup tax; the function’s contract is its signature. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: df['x'].apply(f) vs a vectorized equivalent: the difference is:
cards.back: **apply still loops in Python; vectorized ops execute in compiled C — often 10-100x faster** — apply is a disguised Python loop; true vectorization pushes the loop into C. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Silent type coercion in pandas (e.g. mixed-type columns becoming object) is dangerous because:
cards.back: **Downstream ops behave unexpectedly — a numeric column of strings sorts and sums wrong** — Object dtype hides the problem until an aggregation produces nonsense. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **DataFrame** — pandas' two-dimensional labeled table; the working surface of nearly every wrangling interview question.
- **split-apply-combine** — The groupby grammar: split rows into groups, apply an aggregation or transform, combine the result; expressed as df.groupby(...).agg/transform/filter.
- **merge cardinality** — The expected key uniqueness of a join (one-to-one, many-to-one); asserting it with validate= turns silent fan-out into a loud error.
- **fan-out** — Row multiplication from a many-to-many merge; the classic silent metric corruptor.
- **pivot / melt** — Reshaping between wide and long: pivot spreads values into columns, melt gathers columns into rows.
- **vectorization** — Whole-column operations executed in compiled C (NumPy/pandas internals) instead of Python row loops; typically 10–100x faster and shorter.
- **chunksize** — Reading a file in bounded row chunks so a dataset bigger than memory is processed incrementally.
- **naive vs aware datetimes** — Naive timestamps carry no timezone; aware ones do. Mixing them raises errors, and arithmetic across DST transitions on local time is ambiguous.
- **UTC storage** — The convention of persisting timestamps in UTC and converting to local time only at display; eliminates DST ambiguity at rest.
- **type coercion** — pandas silently casting mixed-type columns to object dtype; downstream ops then sort and sum wrong with no error.
- **pure transform function** — A deterministic function of its inputs with no side effects; testable as plain input/output pairs with no mocks.
- **missingness mechanism** — Why data is missing (MCAR/MAR/MNAR); the diagnosis that decides whether to drop, impute, or flag.

Sources for this module:
- **pandas Documentation** (https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/) — DataFrame reference and user guide: the wrangling half of every data interview.
- **Python Documentation** (https://docs.python.org/3/) — The language reference for the coding reps: data structures, stdlib, and idioms.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
The coding-screen half of data engineering: turning messy extracts into clean tables, in code an interviewer can follow.

The wrangling drill: every exercise starts with a messy extract and ends with a tested, vectorized transform. Work in passes — profile, clean, reshape, verify — and narrate the cleaning decisions out loud, because interviewers grade the judgment, not just the output.
1. Profile first: df.shape, df.dtypes, df.isna().sum(), duplicated().sum(). State what you see before touching anything.
2. Fix types explicitly: pd.to_datetime with a format, astype with errors='raise' thinking — never let silent coercion decide.
3. Localize datetimes to UTC on ingest (tz_localize / tz_convert); do all arithmetic in UTC and convert to local only for display.
4. Reshape with vectorized ops: groupby-agg-transform, boolean masks, np.where, string methods. If you type iterrows, stop and rewrite.
5. Merge defensively: check key uniqueness on both sides first, then merge with validate='m:1' (or the expected cardinality) so fan-out fails loudly.
6. For files bigger than memory: read with chunksize or usecols, aggregate incrementally, and downcast dtypes; never assume the data fits.
7. Wrap the transform in a pure function and write input/output assertions for the edge cases: nulls, dupes, DST boundaries.

import pandas as pd

def clean_orders(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    out = df.copy()
    out['order_ts'] = pd.to_datetime(out['order_ts'], utc=True)  # aware, UTC
    out = out.drop_duplicates(subset=['order_id'])
    # defensive merge: expect many orders to one customer
    out = out.merge(customers, on='customer_id', validate='m:1')
    # vectorized: no row loops
    out['is_weekend'] = out['order_ts'].dt.dayofweek >= 5
    return out

# chunked read for files bigger than memory

cards.front: Full vs incremental extraction — how do you choose?
cards.back: Full: simple, correct, expensive — fine for small dimensions. Incremental: extract since last watermark (updated_at, CDC) — cheap, but needs late-arrival handling and idempotent loads. The interview line: ‘incremental is an optimization with a correctness contract.’

cards.front: How do you discuss Airflow DAG design?
cards.back: DAGs as code: tasks are operators, dependencies define the graph, sensors wait on external state, retries with backoff handle transient failure, and SLA/alerting covers the on-call reality. The interview probes: idempotency (safe reruns) and backfill strategy.

cards.front: Spark: partitions, shuffles, and skew — the interview version?
cards.back: Partitions are the parallelism unit; shuffles (repartitioning data across the network) are the expensive operation; skew (one giant key) kills parallelism. Fixes: salting skewed keys, broadcast joins for small tables, and repartitioning deliberately.

cards.front: How do you explain idempotency to an interviewer?
cards.back: ‘Safe to retry’: repeating the request doesn’t change the outcome beyond the first application. Design it with idempotency keys on writes, and pair it with safe retries (exponential backoff + jitter) for distributed calls.

cards.front: What data-quality checks go inside a pipeline?
cards.back: Freshness (did it arrive?), volume (row counts in range?), schema (columns/types as expected?), distribution (nulls, dupes, outliers vs history). Fail the batch or quarantine it — never silently pass bad data to stakeholders.

cards.front: What's the interview line for choosing incremental extraction?
cards.back: 'Incremental is an optimization with a correctness contract': you save cost but owe the system a watermark, late-arrival handling, and idempotent loads. If you can't name the contract, you don't get the optimization.

cards.front: Backfills: what makes them safe versus dangerous?
cards.back: Safe backfills are idempotent and scoped: deterministic date-partition writes, MERGE or overwrite of exactly the rerun window, and a pre-flight check of what downstream will recompute. Dangerous backfills rerun open-ended ranges into non-idempotent sinks with no dry run. The line: 'I backfill by partition, never by vibes.'

cards.front: How do you answer 'design a daily pipeline' end-to-end?
cards.back: Structure it aloud: source and extraction (full vs incremental by source capability), landing (raw immutable files by date partition), transform (validated staging to modeled tables), load (idempotent writes with DQ gates), orchestration (DAG with retries and SLA), and observability (row counts, freshness, alerts). cards.front: A volume check catches:

cards.front: An idempotency key on a payment endpoint protects against:
cards.back: **Double-charging when the client retries a timed-out request** — The server recognizes the retried key and returns the original result instead of charging again. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Data skew hurts Spark because:
cards.back: **One partition holds most data — straggler tasks bottleneck the stage** — Parallelism is only as fast as the slowest partition; skew serializes the job. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Airflow retries help with:
cards.back: **Transient failures (flaky APIs, brief outages) — with backoff between attempts** — Retries assume the failure is temporary; deterministic bugs need a code fix, not retries. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **full extraction** — Reloading the entire source each run: simple and correct, expensive at scale; the right default for small dimensions.
- **incremental extraction** — Pulling only what changed since a watermark (updated_at, CDC stream): cheap, but needs late-arrival handling and idempotent loads — 'an optimization with a correctness contract.'
- **watermark** — The high-water mark of processed data (a timestamp or offset); everything after it is new, everything before it is assumed complete.
- **DAG (directed acyclic graph)** — Airflow's unit of orchestration: tasks as operators, edges as dependencies; cycles are forbidden so execution order is always resolvable.
- **sensor** — An Airflow operator that waits for external state (a file landing, a partition ready) before downstream tasks run.
- **idempotency** — Safe to retry: repeating an operation doesn't change the outcome beyond the first application; designed with idempotency keys and partition-scoped writes.
- **backfill** — Reprocessing a historical range after a bug or late data; done partition-scoped and throttled, with a runbook — 'production changes with a plan.'
- **partition (Spark)** — The unit of parallelism: data split across workers; too few partitions starves cores, too many drowns in overhead.
- **shuffle** — Repartitioning data across the network (groupBy, join on unpartitioned keys): the most expensive Spark operation, to be minimized deliberately.
- **skew** — One key holding most of the data, so one partition becomes the straggler that bottlenecks the whole stage; fixed by salting keys or broadcast joins.
- **broadcast join** — Replicating a small table to every worker to avoid shuffling the large one; the standard skew-adjacent optimization.
- **data-quality gate** — An in-pipeline check (freshness, volume, schema, distribution) that fails or quarantines a batch instead of silently passing bad data downstream.
- **SLA / alerting** — The on-call contract: how late is too late, who gets paged, and what the runbook says — interviewers probe this because pipelines are operated, not just built.

Sources for this module:
- **Apache Airflow Documentation** (https://airflow.apache.org/docs/) — Workflow orchestration reference: DAGs, operators, sensors, and retries.
- **Apache Spark Documentation** (https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/) — Distributed data processing reference: partitions, shuffles, and the DataFrame API.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
How to whiteboard a pipeline end to end: where the data lands, how it moves, what breaks, and how you know. The system-design core of the DE interview.

The whiteboard drill: given a vague 'design a pipeline' prompt, run the same sequence every time — scope, sketch, walk the data, break it, monitor it. Reps are timed at 30 minutes; the narration is the deliverable.
1. Scope the problem in the first 3 minutes: sources, volume, freshness requirement, consumers. State the latency need — it decides batch vs streaming.
2. Draw the stages left to right: extract -> land (raw) -> transform -> serve. Name the storage at each stage and the grain of the data there.
3. Choose extraction: full for small dimensions, incremental with a watermark for large fact sources; name the late-arrival plan.
4. Design orchestration: DAG shape, sensors on external dependencies, retries with backoff for transient failures, SLA and alerting for the on-call reality.
5. Walk a record through the system aloud; then break it: kill the source mid-run, skew one key, deliver late data. Name what each failure does and which gate catches it.
6. Add the DQ gates: freshness (did it arrive?), volume (counts in band?), schema (shape as expected?), distribution (nulls/dupes/outliers vs history). Fail or quarantine — never silently pass.
7. Close with the backfill runbook: partition-scoped reruns, throttling, validation against the original run's metrics, and rollback criteria.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Design and document a batch pipeline for daily e-commerce reporting: orders and clickstream land as raw files, get modeled into a warehouse, and serve a revenue dashboard. Deliverables: (1) an architecture diagram (stages, storage, grain at each stage), (2) an Airflow DAG skeleton with tasks, sensors, retries, and SLA, (3) the DQ gate list with thresholds and fail-vs-quarantine decisions, (4) a backfill runbook for a corrupted 3-day range, and (5) a Spark note: partition strategy, where shuffles occur, and the skew-mitigation plan for the top-1% customer key. Present it as a 30-minute whiteboard talk.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Data interviews test judgment as much as syntax. In Batch Pipeline Design, these habits fail candidates:
- **SQL without thinking in sets.** Row-by-row mental models break on real queries. Think in sets, joins, and aggregations — say the grain of every result out loud.
- **No business framing.** A metric without a decision it informs is trivia. Every analysis in Batch Pipeline Design starts from: what decision does this change?
- **Experiment sloppiness.** Peeking at results, ignoring power, confusing correlation with lift. Design the test before you look at the data.
- **Pretty charts, no insight.** Visualization is argument, not decoration. Every chart needs a title that states the conclusion, not the topic.
- **Can't walk the pipeline end to end.** Knowing the modeling step but not ingestion, validation, or serving. Interviewers probe the seams — own the whole pipeline.
- **Answering before clarifying.** Ambiguous question, instant query. Ask about grain, time window, definitions, and edge cases first — it mirrors the real job.

cards.front: Event time vs processing time?
cards.back: Event time: when it happened (in the data). Processing time: when the system saw it (wall clock). Late/out-of-order data forces the distinction — watermarks bound how long you wait. The interview line: ‘processing time lies about the world; event time tells the truth late.’

cards.front: Offset vs cursor pagination: the interview-ready comparison?
cards.back: Offset is simple but skips/duplicates rows when data changes and gets slower deep into the list; cursor (keyset) pagination is stable and O(1)-ish per page using an indexed column. Choose cursor for feeds, offset for admin UIs.

cards.front: At-least-once vs exactly-once: the honest interview answer?
cards.back: At-least-once is the practical default (retries can duplicate); exactly-once needs idempotent consumers or transactions (Kafka EOS). The strong answer: ‘I design consumers idempotent, so duplicates are harmless — then at-least-once delivery is effectively exactly-once processing.’

cards.front: How do you handle watermarks, late data, and windowing?
cards.back: Windows (tumbling/sliding/session) bound aggregations in event time; watermarks declare lateness tolerance; late data past the watermark goes to a side output or triggers correction. The interview line: ‘every streaming aggregate is a bet about lateness.’

cards.front: Lambda vs Kappa?
cards.back: Lambda: batch + speed layers, serving merged (complex, battle-tested). Kappa: single streaming pipeline, reprocess by replaying the log (simpler, needs a replayable log like Kafka). The interview judgment: Kappa unless you can name why batch is required.

cards.front: What's the interview line for watermarks?
cards.back: 'Every streaming aggregate is a bet about lateness': the watermark is your declared tolerance — how long you wait for stragglers before calling a window complete. Late data past it needs a side output or a correction path.

cards.front: How do you handle schema evolution in streaming?
cards.back: Schema registry with compatibility rules: BACKWARD for new consumers reading old events, FORWARD for old consumers reading new ones. Never break contracts — add optional fields, never rename or remove required ones. The interview line: 'Streams are APIs with infinite uptime; I version the schema like I version an API.'

cards.front: What do you say about stateful stream processing?
cards.back: Stateful operators keep per-key state across events — session windows, running aggregates, dedup buffers. The hard parts are state size (memory/disk), recovery (checkpoints to durable storage), and late data (watermarks bound the wait). The line: 'Stateless transforms are easy; the moment I keep state, I'm designing for recovery.'

cards.front: Kappa architecture simplifies Lambda by:
cards.back: **Using one streaming pipeline with log replay instead of separate batch and speed layers** — If the log is replayable, reprocessing replaces the batch layer entirely. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Tumbling vs sliding windows differ in that:
cards.back: **Tumbling windows don’t overlap; sliding windows overlap by the slide interval** — Overlap determines whether an event contributes to one window or many. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: The most robust way to handle duplicate deliveries is:
cards.back: **Idempotent consumers, so reprocessing is safe** — Duplicates are inevitable in distributed systems; idempotency makes them harmless. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Cursor pagination avoids the ‘missing rows’ problem of offset because:
cards.back: **It pages relative to a stable key instead of a shifting row number** — New inserts shift offsets; a keyset cursor anchors to the last seen key, immune to shifts. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **event time** — When something happened, recorded in the data; the truth about the world, which arrives late and out of order.
- **processing time** — When the system observed the event (wall clock); convenient but 'lies about the world' whenever data is delayed.
- **watermark** — The system's declaration of how late it's willing to wait: event time up to the watermark is considered complete; later data is late.
- **late data** — Events arriving after their window's watermark; handled via allowed lateness, side outputs, or corrective updates — every streaming aggregate is a bet about lateness.
- **tumbling window** — Fixed, non-overlapping time buckets; each event belongs to exactly one window.
- **sliding window** — Overlapping windows advancing by a slide interval; an event contributes to multiple windows.
- **session window** — Activity-based windows split by gaps of inactivity; the right shape for user sessions.
- **topic (Kafka)** — A named, partitioned append-only log; the unit of organization in event streaming.
- **partition (Kafka)** — An ordered, immutable sequence within a topic; the unit of parallelism — one consumer per partition within a group.
- **offset** — A partition's per-record sequence number; consumers commit offsets to track progress, and rewinds replay history.
- **at-least-once** — Delivery with retries: no data lost, duplicates possible; the practical default.
- **exactly-once (processing)** — Each record's effect applied once, achieved via idempotent consumers or transactions (Kafka EOS); the strong answer is 'idempotent consumers make at-least-once delivery effectively exactly-once processing.'
- **Lambda architecture** — Batch layer plus speed layer, serving layer merges both; complex, battle-tested.
- **Kappa architecture** — A single streaming pipeline with log replay replacing the batch layer; simpler, needs a replayable log.

Sources for this module:
- **Apache Kafka Documentation** (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/) — Event streaming reference: topics, partitions, offsets, and delivery semantics.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Streaming as interviewers test it: the semantics vocabulary (delivery guarantees, watermarks, windows) and the judgment call of when streaming is worth the complexity.

The streaming drill: for each scenario, name the semantics before the technology. Interviewers grade whether you reach for streaming for the right reason — the latency requirement — and whether your design survives late data and duplicates.
1. State the freshness requirement first: 'how fresh must the data be for the decision it serves?' If hours are fine, defend batch and stop.
2. Separate event time from processing time; name where late or out-of-order data can enter.
3. Choose windows (tumbling/sliding/session) from the question's shape, and set the watermark as an explicit lateness bet.
4. Design the consumer idempotent (idempotency keys, upserts) so at-least-once delivery is safe; name what breaks under duplicates.
5. Sketch the Kafka layout: topics, partition count from throughput and parallelism needs, consumer groups, offset-commit strategy.
6. Plan replay: offsets rewind, the log is the source of truth — this is what makes Kappa reprocessing possible.
7. Name the failure modes: broker loss, consumer lag, poison pills, watermark stalls — and the monitoring that exposes each.

notes.body: Design a streaming pipeline for real-time fraud alerts on card transactions: events must be scored within 60 seconds of authorization. Defend the complexity: prove minutes matter here.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Data interviews test judgment as much as syntax. In Streaming Systems, these habits fail candidates:
- **SQL without thinking in sets.** Row-by-row mental models break on real queries. Think in sets, joins, and aggregations — say the grain of every result out loud.
- **No business framing.** A metric without a decision it informs is trivia. Every analysis in Streaming Systems starts from: what decision does this change?
- **Experiment sloppiness.** Peeking at results, ignoring power, confusing correlation with lift. Design the test before you look at the data.
- **Pretty charts, no insight.** Visualization is argument, not decoration. Every chart needs a title that states the conclusion, not the topic.
- **Can't walk the pipeline end to end.** Knowing the modeling step but not ingestion, validation, or serving. Interviewers probe the seams — own the whole pipeline.
- **Answering before clarifying.** Ambiguous question, instant query. Ask about grain, time window, definitions, and edge cases first — it mirrors the real job.

quiz.q: Kappa architecture simplifies Lambda by:
choices: Using one streaming pipeline with log replay instead of separate batch and speed layers
quiz.explain: If the log is replayable, reprocessing replaces the batch layer entirely. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: Tumbling vs sliding windows differ in that:
choices: Tumbling windows don’t overlap; sliding windows overlap by the slide interval
quiz.explain: Overlap determines whether an event contributes to one window or many. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: The most robust way to handle duplicate deliveries is:
choices: Preventing all duplicates in the broker
Idempotent consumers, so reprocessing is safe
quiz.explain: Duplicates are inevitable in distributed systems; idempotency makes them harmless. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: Cursor pagination avoids the ‘missing rows’ problem of offset because:
choices: It pages relative to a stable key instead of a shifting row number
quiz.explain: New inserts shift offsets; a keyset cursor anchors to the last seen key, immune to shifts. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: Processing time 'lies about the world' when:
choices: Events arrive late or out of order — observation time no longer reflects occurrence time
quiz.explain: Delayed data makes wall-clock assignment wrong; event time tells the truth, late. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: In Kafka, the unit of parallelism for consumers is the:
choices: Partition — one consumer per partition within a group
quiz.explain: Ordering is per-partition, so scaling consumers means scaling partitions. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: Session windows are split by:
choices: Gaps of inactivity exceeding a threshold — activity defines the window
quiz.explain: Sessions follow behavior, not the clock — a gap ends one session and starts the next. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: The strongest defense against duplicate deliveries is:
choices: Idempotent consumers — reprocessing the same record is harmless
quiz.explain: Duplicates are inevitable in distributed systems; idempotency makes them safe. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: Kappa replaces Lambda's batch layer with:
choices: Log replay — reprocessing the immutable event log through the single streaming pipeline
quiz.explain: If the log is replayable, reprocessing replaces batch entirely — one pipeline to maintain. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: Committing Kafka offsets after processing (rather than before) protects against:
choices: Data loss on crash — uncommitted offsets get replayed
quiz.explain: Commit-after means a crash replays from the last commit: at-least-once, never lost. See the 'Hands-on procedure' in this module.

cards.front: How do you explain a warehouse design in a whiteboard round?
cards.back: Three moves: name the grain of the central fact ('one row per order line'), list the dimensions you'd hang off it (date, customer, product, store), then state the SCD policy per dimension (type 1 for corrections, type 2 for tracked history). Draw the star before you speak. The line: 'Facts hold the grain, dimensions hold the context, and I declare both before drawing anything.'

cards.front: Star vs snowflake?
cards.back: Star: denormalized dimensions (one join to facts — fast, simple). Snowflake: normalized dimensions (less redundancy, more joins). Analytics favors star for query simplicity; the interview follow-up is always ‘choose the grain first.’

cards.front: Slowly changing dimensions, types 1 and 2?
cards.back: Type 1: overwrite (history lost — fine for corrections). Type 2: new row per change with effective dates/current flag (history preserved — the analytics default). The interview question is always ‘do we need history?’ — that answer picks the type.

cards.front: Normalization vs denormalization in warehouse modeling?
cards.back: Normalize for write integrity (one fact, one place); denormalize dimensions for read simplicity (star schema). The interview line: ‘I normalize the facts, denormalize the dimensions — each for its reader.’

cards.front: What’s the bronze/silver/gold (medallion) pattern?
cards.back: Bronze: raw ingested data (immutable, append-only). Silver: cleaned, validated, conformed. Gold: aggregated, business-ready marts. Each layer has a contract; quality gates between layers stop bad data from flowing downstream.

cards.front: What's the interview line for SCD type choice?
cards.back: 'Do we need history?' — Type 1 overwrites (corrections, typos: history lost, correctly). Type 2 versions rows with effective dates (history preserved). The question that picks the type is always about the business need for point-in-time truth.

cards.front: What are conformed, degenerate, and junk dimensions?
cards.back: Conformed dimensions are shared across facts (one Date table for all marts) so metrics agree. Degenerate dimensions are dimensional attributes with no own table — like order number — parked directly on the fact. Junk dimensions bundle low-cardinality flags (yes/no codes) into one table to avoid a dozen tiny dims. The line: 'Conform so numbers agree, degenerate what's unique, junk what’s trivial.'

cards.front: How do you handle late-arriving facts in a warehouse design?
cards.back: Late facts land after the partition was built — restatements, corrections, delayed feeds. The design answer: restatable partitions (recompute the window, don't patch in place), a 'processed-as-of' watermark so consumers know the revision, and idempotent merges. The line: 'Late data is a restatement, not an edit — I rebuild the partition and stamp the revision.'

cards.front: dbt tests primarily assert:
cards.back: **Data contracts — uniqueness, not-null, referential integrity on every model** — Tests turn assumptions about the data into verified guarantees on each run. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Data-quality checks belong:
cards.back: **At layer boundaries — especially bronze→silver, so bad data never flows downstream** — Gates between medallion layers quarantine bad data where it’s cheapest to fix. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Star schemas denormalize dimensions because:
cards.back: **Analytics queries read dimensions constantly — fewer joins, simpler queries, faster BI** — Read-optimized modeling: the query pattern (not write purity) rules the warehouse. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: SCD Type 2 preserves history by:
cards.back: **Adding a new dimension row per change with effective dates** — Versioned rows with date ranges: point-in-time analysis stays correct. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **fact table** — Measurements of business events (orders, clicks): narrow, long, numeric, joined to dimensions; the grain question is always asked here first.
- **dimension table** — Descriptive context (customer, product, date): wide, denormalized in a star schema, the 'who/what/where' of each fact.
- **grain** — The business-event level of a fact table (one row per order line); every modeling decision flows from declaring it explicitly.
- **star schema** — Denormalized dimensions joined directly to the fact table: fewer joins, simpler queries, faster BI — the analytics default.
- **snowflake schema** — Normalized dimensions (dimension tables referencing other dimension tables): less redundancy, more joins; chosen when storage or write-integrity dominates.
- **SCD Type 1** — Overwrite the dimension attribute; history is lost — correct for corrections and typos.
- **SCD Type 2** — New dimension row per change with effective dates and a current flag; history preserved — the analytics default whenever 'what did we know then?' matters.
- **normalization** — Organizing data to reduce redundancy and protect write integrity; the OLTP virtue, applied to facts.
- **denormalization** — Deliberate redundancy for read simplicity and speed; the warehouse virtue, applied to dimensions.
- **bronze layer** — Raw ingested data, immutable and append-only; the system's memory of what actually arrived.
- **silver layer** — Cleaned, validated, conformed data; quality gates sit at the bronze-to-silver boundary.
- **gold layer** — Aggregated, business-ready marts and metrics; what BI and stakeholders consume.
- **dbt model** — A versioned SQL transform with tests and documentation as code; the analytics-engineering unit of warehouse work.
- **dbt test** — Data contracts as code: uniqueness, not-null, referential integrity asserted on every run.

Sources for this module:
- **Kimball Group** (https://www.kimballgroup.com/) — The dimensional-modeling home: facts, dimensions, grain, and slowly changing dimensions.
- **dbt Documentation** (https://docs.getdbt.com/) — Analytics-engineering reference: models, tests, and docs as code on top of the warehouse.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Modeling is where DE interviews separate memorizers from thinkers: grain decisions, SCD handling, and why the warehouse is shaped the way it is.

The modeling drill: every exercise starts from a business question and ends at a declared grain. Interviewers don't grade the diagram's beauty — they grade whether you asked 'what's the grain?' before drawing anything.
1. Restate the business question and name the measurable event: what happened, to whom, when.
2. Declare the grain explicitly ('one row per order line') and defend it — everything downstream depends on this sentence.
3. Identify facts (the numbers) vs dimensions (the context); list the dimension attributes the question's slices need.
4. Choose star vs snowflake: default to star for analytics; reach for snowflake only when you can name the redundancy or write-integrity reason.
5. For each dimension that changes, pick the SCD type: Type 1 for corrections, Type 2 when history must survive — the interview question is always 'do we need history?'
6. Layer it bronze/silver/gold: raw landing, conformed cleaning with gates, business-ready marts. Name the contract each layer promises.
7. Write the dbt-style tests for the model: uniqueness on keys, not-null on required columns, referential integrity to dimensions — contracts, not hopes.
notes.code:
-- SCD Type 2: preserve history with effective dates
SELECT customer_key,
       customer_id,
       segment,
       effective_from,
       effective_to,
       is_current
FROM dim_customer
WHERE '2026-01-15' BETWEEN effective_from
      AND COALESCE(effective_to, '9999-12-31');  -- point-in-time correct

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Model a warehouse for a subscription SaaS: signups, plans, invoices, cancellations, and product usage events. Deliverables: (1) a declared grain per fact table with the reasoning, (2) a star schema diagram (facts, dimensions, keys), (3) SCD decisions per changing dimension with the 'do we need history?' justification, (4) the bronze/silver/gold layering with the contract each layer promises, and (5) dbt-style model tests (uniqueness, not-null, relationships). Present the model as a 20-minute whiteboard walkthrough ending with: 'what breaks if the grain is wrong?'

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Preparation, not a credential: this module confers no certificate and makes no placement claims. Dimensional modeling is a mature discipline — the principles here are stable — but every company's warehouse has its own conventions; interviews test your reasoning about grain and history, not allegiance to one school.

notes.title: Worked example: dbt tests primarily assert:
notes.body:
**Problem.** dbt tests primarily assert:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Data contracts — uniqueness, not-null, referential integrity on every model
- **Why:** Tests turn assumptions about the data into verified guarantees on each run. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Tests turn assumptions about the data into verified guarantees on each run.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

cards.front: How do you run a safe backfill?
cards.back: Idempotent stages, partition-scoped reruns (not full-table), throttled to protect production, validated against the original run’s metrics, with a runbook: what, why, scope, rollback. The interview line: ‘backfills are production changes with a plan.’

cards.front: How do you narrate design decisions aloud?
cards.back: Decision → alternatives considered → why this one (constraint it satisfies) → what would change your mind. The interview line: ‘I narrate the tradeoff, not just the choice — the reasoning is what’s being graded.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'End-to-end batch pipeline from raw files'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: For 'Modeled warehouse layer with tested transforms', what’s the tradeoff question you should answer before the interviewer asks it?
cards.back: Every technique has a cost: name what you gain, what you pay, and when you’d choose the alternative. ‘It depends’ is only a good answer when you then explain what it depends on.

cards.front: How do you turn 'Data-quality gates and reconciliation checks' into a story the interviewer remembers?
cards.back: Anchor it to a decision: ‘we chose X over Y because…’ Interviewers probe decisions, not definitions — one concrete tradeoff you navigated beats three textbook paragraphs.

cards.front: What makes a capstone defensible in an interview?
cards.back: Every choice has a stated reason and a named alternative: 'we chose X over Y because...' plus a runbook, DQ gates, and a reconciliation check. Interviewers probe decisions, not definitions — the decision log is the artifact they're really reading.

cards.front: How do you discuss monitoring and SLAs for the pipeline?
cards.back: Three signals: freshness (did today's partition land by the SLA?), volume (row counts vs expectation), and correctness (DQ checks green). Define the SLA up front — 'data ready by 7am for the 9am reports' — then show the alert path when it breaks. The line: 'A pipeline without an SLA is a script; I define ready, then I prove it.'

cards.front: What does reproducibility mean for a capstone pipeline?
cards.back: Same inputs, same code, same outputs — pinned dependencies, seeded randomness, immutable raw landing, and versioned transforms. If the reviewer reruns it next week they must get the same tables. The line: 'I defend reproducibility like a scientist: pinned code, frozen inputs, documented environment.'

cards.front: Narrating rejected alternatives is strong because:
cards.back: **It proves you see the design space — choices are only meaningful against options** — A decision without visible alternatives looks like a guess; with them, it’s engineering. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Backfills must be partition-scoped because:
cards.back: **Rerunning everything wastes cost and risks touching good data — scope to what’s wrong** — Surgical reruns: fix the affected range, leave correct history alone. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: You’re asked about 'End-to-end batch pipeline from raw files' and your memory blanks. What’s the strongest recovery?
cards.back: **State what you do know precisely, name the boundary, and reason from first principles aloud** — Interviewers score honesty + reasoning: a precise partial answer with clear boundaries beats a confident fabrication every time. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: The interviewer pushes back on your 'Modeled warehouse layer with tested transforms' answer. Best response?
cards.back: **Steel-man their objection, check it against your reasoning aloud, and update or hold with evidence** — Pushback tests intellectual honesty: engage the objection seriously, reason aloud, and let evidence decide. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **capstone artifact** — A complete, documented build you can walk an interviewer through; evidence beats narrative in every loop.
- **end-to-end lineage** — The traceable path from raw source to served metric: every transformation named, every stage's contract stated.
- **runbook** — The written procedure for operating and recovering the pipeline: backfills, reruns, rollback — 'backfills are production changes with a plan.'
- **reconciliation check** — Comparing pipeline outputs against independent totals (source counts, prior runs) to prove completeness.
- **architecture decision record** — Decision, alternatives considered, why this one, what would change your mind — the format for narrating design aloud.
- **data contract** — The explicit promise between pipeline stages or producers and consumers: schema, grain, freshness, quality thresholds.
- **observability** — Freshness, volume, and distribution signals that tell you the pipeline is healthy without reading logs.
- **defensible design** — A design whose every choice has a stated reason and a named alternative; what 'narrate the tradeoff, not just the choice' produces.

Sources for this module:
- **Apache Airflow Documentation** (https://airflow.apache.org/docs/) — Workflow orchestration reference: DAGs, operators, sensors, and retries.
- **dbt Documentation** (https://docs.getdbt.com/) — Analytics-engineering reference: models, tests, and docs as code on top of the warehouse.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
One pipeline you built, documented, and can defend: the artifact that turns 'tell me about a pipeline' from a story into evidence.

The capstone build sequence: one pipeline, built in order, each stage verified before the next. Work in vertical slices — a thin end-to-end path first — then harden. The README is written as you go, not after.
1. Pick the dataset and the business question it answers; attach a decision to the question so you know when the pipeline is 'done.'
2. Land raw files in bronze: immutable, append-only, with ingestion metadata (source, timestamp, row counts).
3. Build the silver transforms as named, testable stages (clean -> conform -> model); write the grain comment on every model.
4. Add DQ gates at the bronze-to-silver boundary: freshness, volume bands, schema checks, null/dup distribution vs history. Fail or quarantine — never silently pass.
5. Serve the gold layer: the aggregated tables behind one concrete stakeholder question; reconcile outputs against source totals.
6. Write the backfill and rerun runbook: partition scope, throttling, validation against the original run, rollback criteria.
7. Draw the architecture diagram and write the README: data flow, grain per stage, decisions with alternatives, and the five-minute narration script.
8. Rehearse the walkthrough aloud: decision -> alternatives -> why this one -> what would change your mind. Time it at 15 minutes.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Deliver the capstone: an end-to-end batch pipeline over a public or synthetic e-commerce dataset. The repository must contain: raw ingestion to bronze, tested silver transforms with declared grains, DQ gates with thresholds, a gold serving layer answering one stakeholder question, a reconciliation check against source totals, a backfill runbook, an architecture diagram, and a README with the decision log. The final deliverable is a 15-minute recorded or live walkthrough: narrate the tradeoffs, name the failure modes, show a gate catching bad data. This is the portfolio piece you link when they ask for pipeline experience.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Preparation, not a credential: this module confers no certificate and makes no placement claims. A capstone proves you can build and reason about a pipeline — it doesn't substitute for production experience, and interviewers will probe the gap honestly. Claim only what the artifact demonstrates; the decision log is where your real thinking shows.

notes.title: Worked example: Narrating rejected alternatives is strong because:
notes.body:
**Problem.** Narrating rejected alternatives is strong because:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** It proves you see the design space — choices are only meaningful against options
- **Why:** A decision without visible alternatives looks like a guess; with them, it’s engineering. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *A decision without visible alternatives looks like a guess; with them, it’s engineering.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Data interviews test judgment as much as syntax. In Pipeline Capstone, these habits fail candidates:
- **SQL without thinking in sets.** Row-by-row mental models break on real queries. Think in sets, joins, and aggregations — say the grain of every result out loud.
- **No business framing.** A metric without a decision it informs is trivia. Every analysis in Pipeline Capstone starts from: what decision does this change?
- **Experiment sloppiness.** Peeking at results, ignoring power, confusing correlation with lift. Design the test before you look at the data.
- **Pretty charts, no insight.** Visualization is argument, not decoration. Every chart needs a title that states the conclusion, not the topic.
- **Can't walk the pipeline end to end.** Knowing the modeling step but not ingestion, validation, or serving. Interviewers probe the seams — own the whole pipeline.
- **Answering before clarifying.** Ambiguous question, instant query. Ask about grain, time window, definitions, and edge cases first — it mirrors the real job.

cards.front: How do you handle timed SQL rounds?
cards.back: The 15-minute playbook: clarify grain (1 min), sketch CTE stages aloud (2 min), write in passes, verify on a mental dataset, narrate throughout. The interview line: ‘method is the deliverable — the query is just evidence.’

cards.front: How do you handle framework whiteboard rounds?
cards.back: Narrate the architecture as you draw: components, lifecycles, data flow — then zoom into the probed area. The interview line: ‘I draw the system first so we both know where the deep dive lives.’

cards.front: How do you debug a broken pipeline in an interview?
cards.back: Narrow systematically: is it extraction, transform, or load? Check the stage’s contract (row counts, schema, DQ gates) — the failing contract names the culprit. The interview line: ‘pipelines fail at stage boundaries; I check the contracts.’

cards.front: How do you argue batch vs streaming tradeoffs?
cards.back: From the latency requirement: batch wins on simplicity, cost, and correctness-ease; streaming wins when minutes matter. Name both sides’ costs honestly. The interview line: ‘I argue from the requirement, not from enthusiasm.’

cards.front: How do you tell the data-incident story?
cards.back: STAR with data texture: the bad data, who consumed it, the blast radius, how you quarantined and fixed it, and the DQ gate you added so it can’t recur. The interview line: ‘every data incident ends with a gate.’

cards.front: What does the rubric actually measure?
cards.back: Correctness, complexity stated, communication, time management — scored per round, immediately after. The misses go down verbatim and become dated redrill tasks. The rubric turns 'I did badly' into 'I lost points on narration in round 2, redrill Thursday.'

cards.front: How do you handle a question you genuinely don't know?
cards.back: Say so in one sentence, then reason out loud: state your best guess, name what would confirm it, and propose how you'd verify in practice (docs, experiment, EXPLAIN). Interviewers score reasoning under uncertainty higher than a confident bluff. The line: 'I don't know — but here's how I'd figure it out, and here's what I'd check first.'

cards.front: What should you ask the interviewer about the data stack?
cards.back: Ask what reveals the real job: data volume and velocity, the orchestration and warehouse stack, who owns DQ when it breaks, and what the team's biggest pipeline pain is right now. Two or three sharp questions beat ten generic ones. The line: 'I ask about their biggest pipeline pain — it tells me what they're really hiring for.'

cards.front: A redrill plan is effective when it is:
cards.back: **Specific, dated, and tied to named misses from the scored review** — Specificity turns review into training; vague plans evaporate. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Ending with the added DQ gate is strong because:
cards.back: **It proves systemic learning — the incident produced prevention, not just a fix** — Prevention is the deliverable; the fix was just the homework. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: The deciding question in batch vs streaming is:
cards.back: **‘How fresh must the data be for the decision it serves?’ — latency need sets the architecture** — Freshness requirements are the only honest arbiter; everything else is preference. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Checking stage contracts (counts/schema) first works because:
cards.back: **Each stage promises an output shape — the broken promise localizes the bug** — Contract violations pinpoint the stage; log-diving without them is wandering. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **mock circuit** — A full simulated interview loop (SQL screen, system design, debugging, behavioral) run under real timing with scoring rubrics.
- **rubric** — The explicit scoring dimensions: correctness, complexity stated, communication, time management; what 'scored review' measures against.
- **timed SQL round** — Live query writing against the clock; graded on method (grain stated, stages sketched, narration) as much as the final query.
- **whiteboard round** — System-design narration while drawing: components, data flow, failure modes; 'draw the system first so we both know where the deep dive lives.'
- **debugging scenario** — A broken pipeline presented as a symptom; graded on systematic narrowing (extract/transform/load, stage contracts) over log-diving.
- **tradeoff argument** — The batch-vs-streaming style debate: arguing from the requirement (latency, cost, complexity) with both sides' costs named honestly.
- **incident story** — The behavioral artifact: bad data, blast radius, quarantine, fix, and the DQ gate added so it can't recur — 'every data incident ends with a gate.'
- **redrill plan** — Misses from scored review converted into specific, dated practice tasks; 'three sliding-window problems, timed, by Thursday' — not 'practice more.'

Sources for this module:
- **DataLemur** (https://datalemur.com) — SQL and data interview questions in the style real screens ask them; used for timed reps, not answers.
- **Apache Spark Documentation** (https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/) — Distributed data processing reference: partitions, shuffles, and the DataFrame API.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Full interview simulations with scoring rubrics: the pressure reps that convert knowledge into performance.

The mock protocol: simulate the real loop as closely as pressure allows — same timing, same narration demand, same rubric. One full circuit per session, then scored review, then redrills. No pausing the clock to think; the clock is the point.
1. Set up the circuit: 15-minute SQL screen, 30-minute pipeline whiteboard, 15-minute debugging scenario, 10-minute incident story. Timer visible, no pauses.
2. Run the SQL round with the playbook: grain (1 min), CTE stages aloud (2 min), write in passes, verify on a mental dataset, narrate throughout.
3. Run the whiteboard: draw components and data flow first, then deep-dive where probed; narrate tradeoffs and name rejected alternatives.
4. Run the debugging scenario: narrow by stage (extract/transform/load), check each stage's contract (counts, schema, gates) — the broken promise names the culprit.
5. Tell the incident story in STAR with data texture: the bad data, who consumed it, blast radius, quarantine, fix, and the gate you added.
6. Score every round against the rubric immediately after: correctness, complexity stated, communication, time. Write the misses down verbatim.
7. Convert each miss into a dated redrill task before the next circuit; the plan is specific and scheduled, or it evaporates.

notes.body: Run and document three full mock circuits over two weeks. cards.front: Which distributions must you know cold, and when?
cards.back: Normal (means, CLT-backed inference), binomial (counts of yes/no), Poisson (event rates over time/space). The interview line: ‘I match the distribution to the data-generating process, not to habit.’

cards.front: How do you reason about expectation and variance in interviews?
cards.back: Expectation is linear (E[aX+bY] = aE[X]+bE[Y] — no independence needed); variance adds only for independent variables. Conditioning (E[X|Y]) is how you slice: the interview line is ‘condition on what you know, average over what you don’t.’

cards.front: Explain the central limit theorem plainly.
cards.back: Averages of many independent samples become approximately normal regardless of the underlying distribution — which is why confidence intervals and z-tests work on real data. The interview caveat: ‘independent’ and ‘enough samples’ are doing heavy lifting.

cards.front: How do you explain a confidence interval without mysticism?
cards.back: ‘If we repeated this procedure many times, ~95% of the intervals would contain the true value.’ It’s about the procedure’s long-run behavior, not ‘95% chance the truth is in this one.’ Wider interval = more uncertainty.

cards.front: What does a p-value actually say?
cards.back: The probability of seeing data this extreme if the null were true — NOT the probability the null is true, and not the size of the effect. The interview line: ‘p-values measure surprise under the null, nothing more.’

cards.front: What's the interview line for the base-rate trap?
cards.back: 'A 99%-accurate test for a 0.1%-prevalent disease still yields mostly false positives — Bayes' rule says the base rate dominates.' The interview line: 'I never interpret a test result without the prevalence.'

cards.front: How do you explain Bayes' rule in a DS interview?
cards.back: Bayes updates beliefs: posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence. Plain version: start with a base rate, update with how likely the new evidence is under each hypothesis. Use the medical-test example to show base rates dominating. The line: 'Bayes is just disciplined updating — prior belief, new evidence, revised belief.'

cards.front: When do you bootstrap instead of using formulas?
cards.back: When the statistic has no clean formula — medians, ratios, custom business metrics — or when assumptions (normality, large n) look shaky. Resample with replacement, recompute the statistic thousands of times, read the interval off the distribution. The line: 'If I can simulate the sampling distribution, I don't need the formula's assumptions.'

cards.front: A 99%-accurate test for a 0.1%-prevalent disease: most positives are false because:
cards.back: **Base rate: even 1% error on 99.9% healthy people swamps the true positives** — Bayes: P(disease|positive) depends on prevalence — rare conditions make false positives dominate. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: p = 0.03 means:
cards.back: **If the null were true, you’d see results this extreme 3% of the time** — It’s a conditional probability under the null — a common misreading is treating it as P(null is true). Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: A 95% confidence interval means:
cards.back: **The procedure captures the true parameter in ~95% of repeated samples** — Frequentist intervals describe the method’s long-run coverage, not a probability about this interval. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: The CLT justifies:
cards.back: **Using normal-based confidence intervals on sample means from non-normal data (with enough samples)** — Sample means converge to normal as n grows — the foundation of classical inference on means. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.
