notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **normal distribution** — The bell curve parameterized by mean and variance; the limit shape of sample means via the CLT, and the backbone of classical inference.
- **binomial distribution** — Counts of successes in n independent yes/no trials; the model for conversion counts and click tallies.
- **Poisson distribution** — Counts of events over time or space at a constant rate; the model for arrivals, errors per hour, requests per minute.
- **expectation** — The long-run average; linear (E[aX+bY] = aE[X]+bE[Y]) with no independence required — the workhorse identity of interview probability.
- **variance** — Expected squared deviation from the mean; adds across variables only when they're independent.
- **conditioning** — E[X|Y]: slicing expectation by what you know; 'condition on what you know, average over what you don't.'
- **central limit theorem (CLT)** — Averages of many independent samples become approximately normal regardless of the underlying distribution — why normal-based confidence intervals work on real data; 'independent' and 'enough samples' do the heavy lifting.
- **confidence interval** — A procedure with long-run coverage: ~95% of such intervals from repeated samples contain the true parameter — not '95% chance the truth is in this one.'
- **p-value** — The probability of seeing data this extreme if the null were true; NOT the probability the null is true, and not the size of the effect — 'p-values measure surprise under the null, nothing more.'
- **hypothesis test** — A decision procedure with controlled error rates: reject the null when the p-value crosses the pre-chosen significance level.
- **Bayes' rule** — P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B): updating beliefs with evidence; the tool for base-rate problems like the '99%-accurate test' trap.
- **base rate** — The prevalence of the condition in the population; ignoring it makes even accurate tests produce mostly false positives for rare conditions.

Sources for this module:
- **A leading free learning platform: Statistics & Probability** (https://www.khanacademy.org/math) — Free, rigorous statistics floor: distributions, inference, and hypothesis testing.
- **Seeing Theory** (https://seeing-theory.brown.edu) — A visual introduction to probability and statistics; builds the intuition the formulas assume.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
The probability floor every DS interview stands on: distributions, inference, and the discipline of saying exactly what a p-value means.

The stats drill: definitions with intuition, then the caveat, then a number. Every concept gets a tiny worked example — interviewers trust candidates who can compute, not just recite.
1. State the definition precisely, in one sentence, before any intuition.
2. Give the intuition: what the concept measures in plain language.
3. Name the caveat unprompted: independence for the CLT, 'under the null' for p-values, the base rate for Bayes.
4. Work a tiny numeric example (a 2x2 table, ten coin flips) — compute it, don't gesture at it.
5. Connect to the interview use: which DS question this concept answers (sizing a test, reading a result, catching a fallacy).
6. Red-team your own statement: what would make it false? Say it before the interviewer does.

notes.title: Worked example: A 99%-accurate test for a 0.1%-prevalent disease: most positives are…
notes.body:
**Problem.** A 99%-accurate test for a 0.1%-prevalent disease: most positives are false because:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Base rate: even 1% error on 99.9% healthy people swamps the true positives
- **Why:** Bayes: P(disease|positive) depends on prevalence — rare conditions make false positives dominate. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Bayes: P(disease|positive) depends on prevalence — rare conditions make false positives dominate.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Data interviews test judgment as much as syntax. In Statistics and Probability, these habits fail candidates:
- **SQL without thinking in sets.** Row-by-row mental models break on real queries. Think in sets, joins, and aggregations — say the grain of every result out loud.
- **No business framing.** A metric without a decision it informs is trivia. Every analysis in Statistics and Probability starts from: what decision does this change?
- **Experiment sloppiness.** Peeking at results, ignoring power, confusing correlation with lift. Design the test before you look at the data.
- **Pretty charts, no insight.** Visualization is argument, not decoration. Every chart needs a title that states the conclusion, not the topic.
- **Can't walk the pipeline end to end.** Knowing the modeling step but not ingestion, validation, or serving. Interviewers probe the seams — own the whole pipeline.
- **Answering before clarifying.** Ambiguous question, instant query. Ask about grain, time window, definitions, and edge cases first — it mirrors the real job.

cards.front: How do you make exploratory testing rigorous?
cards.back: Charters: time-boxed missions with a goal (‘explore checkout with invalid inputs for 45 minutes’), session notes, and debriefs. It’s skilled investigation, not random clicking — the charter makes it repeatable and reportable.

cards.front: What groupby patterns must be fluent?
cards.back: Aggregations (sum/mean/count per group), transforms (broadcast group stats back to rows), filters (keep groups meeting a condition), and multi-key groupbys. The interview line: ‘split-apply-combine is the grammar of exploratory analysis.’

cards.front: How do you merge without fan-out disasters?
cards.back: Check key uniqueness on both sides first (one-to-many is fine; many-to-many explodes). Validate with row-count assertions before/after, and use validate='m:1' in pandas to enforce expectations loudly.

cards.front: How do you handle missing and messy data?
cards.back: Diagnose the mechanism (MCAR/MAR/MNAR), then choose: drop (if MCAR and plentiful), impute (median/model — and record it), or flag with indicators. The interview line: ‘the missingness is data about the data-generating process.’

cards.front: What does good feature construction look like?
cards.back: Vectorized transforms expressing domain knowledge: ratios, time-since-event, rolling aggregates, encodings of categoricals — built in the pipeline (fit on train only) to avoid leakage. The interview line: ‘features are where domain knowledge becomes model power.’

cards.front: What's the interview line for merge safety?
cards.back: 'I assert cardinality before I trust a merge': check key uniqueness on both sides, merge with validate=, assert row counts before and after. Silent fan-out is the classic way a correct-looking analysis goes wrong.

cards.front: What do you say about outliers — remove or keep?
cards.back: Neither by default: investigate first. Plot them, check if they're data errors (typos, unit mixups) or real signal (fraud, whales). Report both versions if the answer moves. The interview line: 'An outlier is a question, not a deletion — I find out which kind before touching it.'

cards.front: How do you discuss deduplication and record linkage?
cards.back: Exact dedup on keys is the easy case; the real problem is fuzzy duplicates — same entity, different spellings. Name blocking (reduce candidate pairs), string similarity (edit distance), and the manual-review threshold. The line: 'Exact matches dedupe by key; near-matches dedupe by judgment — I quantify both.'

cards.front: Restart-and-run-all validates:
cards.back: **That the notebook has no hidden out-of-order state — true top-to-bottom reproducibility** — Out-of-order execution hides state dependencies; a clean rerun proves the narrative is real. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Building features before the train/test split risks:
cards.back: **Leakage — statistics from the test set contaminating training features** — Any transform that learns from data must be fit on train only, or evaluation is fiction. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Mean imputation’s hidden cost is:
cards.back: **It shrinks variance and distorts relationships — the data looks more certain than it is** — Filling with the mean understates uncertainty; it’s a choice with consequences, not a default. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: pd.merge(validate='m:1') is used to:
cards.back: **Assert the merge keys have the expected uniqueness — failing loudly on fan-out** — Declaring expected cardinality turns silent row multiplication into a loud error. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **EDA (exploratory data analysis)** — Distributions first, then relationships, then data quality; narrated as you go, because live analysis is a thinking test wearing a coding costume.
- **split-apply-combine** — The groupby grammar: aggregations (one row per group), transforms (broadcast group stats back to rows), filters (keep groups meeting a condition).
- **merge validation** — Asserting expected key cardinality (validate='m:1') so fan-out fails loudly instead of silently multiplying rows.
- **fan-out** — Many-to-many merge row multiplication; the silent aggregate corruptor — check key uniqueness on both sides first.
- **missingness mechanism** — MCAR (missing completely at random), MAR, MNAR: the diagnosis that decides drop vs impute vs flag.
- **imputation** — Filling missing values (median, model-based); mean imputation shrinks variance and understates uncertainty — a choice with consequences, not a default.
- **leakage** — Test-set information contaminating training (features fit before the split); makes evaluation fiction — 'fit on train only.'
- **vectorized feature construction** — Building features with whole-column ops (ratios, rolling aggregates, encodings) expressing domain knowledge; 'features are where domain knowledge becomes model power.'
- **reproducible notebook** — Restart-and-run-all clean: no hidden out-of-order state, the narrative is real top-to-bottom.
- **outlier** — An extreme value: investigate before deleting — it may be the signal (fraud) or the noise (sensor glitch); the treatment depends on the cause.

Sources for this module:
- **pandas Documentation** (https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/) — DataFrame reference and user guide: the wrangling half of every data interview.
- **NumPy Documentation** (https://numpy.org/doc/) — Array computing reference under pandas; vectorization is the speed answer.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Analysis as a live-coding skill: from a raw table to an insight, with the pandas idioms interviewers watch for.

The live-analysis drill: every exercise is a raw table and a question, timed at 20 minutes, narrated end to end. The interviewer scores your investigative method — what you check and in what order — so the order is the skill.
1. State the question and the grain before touching the data; write the plan (distributions, relationships, quality) in a markdown cell.
2. Profile: shape, dtypes, missingness, duplicates, basic distributions. Say what surprises you out loud.
3. Check data quality first: row counts vs expectations, impossible values, join-key uniqueness — garbage in, garbage out.
4. Explore distributions per key variable, then relationships (groupby cuts, correlations) — narrate what each plot is testing.
5. Build features vectorized: ratios, time-since-event, rolling aggregates — and fit every learning transform on train only to avoid leakage.
6. Merge only with validated cardinality; assert row counts before and after every join.
7. Finish with restart-and-run-all: the notebook must reproduce top-to-bottom with no hidden state.

# groupby patterns: aggregate, transform, filter

# defensive merge: assert cardinality, check counts
before = len(df)
df = df.merge(dims, on='customer_id', validate='m:1')
assert len(df) == before, 'fan-out detected'

cards.front: How do you discuss regression vs classification interview-style?
cards.back: Regression: predict a number (MSE/MAE, R² with caveats). Classification: predict a class (precision/recall, ROC-AUC, calibration when probabilities matter). The interview line: ‘I start from the decision the prediction serves, then pick the framing.’

cards.front: How do you explain overfitting and its fixes?
cards.back: The model memorizes noise: training error keeps dropping while validation error rises. Fixes: more data, regularization (L1/L2), simpler models, cross-validation for honest measurement, early stopping. The interview line: ‘the validation curve is the truth-teller.’

cards.front: Why three splits?
cards.back: Train: fit. Validation: choose models/hyperparameters (it becomes optimistic through selection). Test: one final unbiased estimate, touched once. The interview trap: tuning on the test set leaks — it’s just validation with extra steps.

cards.front: Precision vs recall — when does each matter?
cards.back: Precision: of flagged items, how many were right (false positives hurt — spam filters). Recall: of real items, how many were caught (false negatives hurt — fraud, disease). ROC-AUC summarizes the tradeoff across thresholds; PR curves are better for imbalanced data.

cards.front: What does feature-engineering judgment look like?
cards.back: Knowing which transforms encode real signal (domain ratios, temporal aggregations) vs noise-fitting, validating with ablations, and watching for leakage. The interview line: ‘a feature is a hypothesis — I test it like one.’

cards.front: What's the interview line for metric choice?
cards.back: 'I start from the decision the prediction serves, then pick the framing': the metric is the business objective, mathematized. Precision when false positives hurt, recall when misses hurt — never the metric I used last time out of habit.

cards.front: When do you prefer logistic regression over a tree model?
cards.back: When interpretability and calibrated probabilities matter more than squeezing accuracy — regulated settings, stakeholder explanations, small data where trees overfit. Say it plainly: simpler wins when the decision must be defended. The line: 'I pick logistic regression when the model has to be argued, not just scored.'

cards.front: How do you discuss class imbalance beyond metrics?
cards.back: Three levers: change the data (class weights, resampling), change the threshold (tune the decision point to the cost matrix), and change the evaluation (PR curves over ROC on skewed data). Always ask what a false negative costs versus a false positive. The line: 'Imbalance is a cost problem first, a sampling problem second.'

cards.front: Naming what would change your mind is strong because:
cards.back: **It proves the choice was reasoned — falsifiability is the mark of real judgment** — A choice you can’t unmake under evidence was never reasoned. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Ablation in feature engineering means:
cards.back: **Removing a feature/group and measuring the performance drop — credit assignment** — Ablations prove a feature earns its keep instead of riding on correlated companions. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: A fraud model needs high recall because:
cards.back: **Missing fraud (false negatives) costs far more than false alarms** — The cost asymmetry decides: when misses are expensive, optimize recall and manage precision. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Tuning hyperparameters on the test set is wrong because:
cards.back: **Repeated selection on the test set makes it optimistic — it’s no longer an unbiased estimate** — The test set must be touched once; every tuning decision on it leaks information into the estimate. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **regression** — Predicting a number (price, demand); evaluated with MSE/MAE and R² (with caveats — it never decreases with more features).
- **classification** — Predicting a class; evaluated with precision/recall, ROC-AUC, and calibration when probabilities drive decisions.
- **overfitting** — The model memorizes noise: training error falls while validation error rises; fought with more data, regularization, simpler models, and honest validation.
- **regularization (L1/L2)** — Penalties on weights: L1 (lasso) drives weights to exactly zero (feature selection); L2 (ridge) shrinks smoothly (handles correlated features).
- **train/validation/test** — Fit on train, select models and hyperparameters on validation, estimate once on test; tuning on test turns it into validation with extra steps.
- **cross-validation** — Rotating validation folds for a stabler performance estimate on small data; still never touches the test set.
- **precision** — Of flagged items, how many were right; the metric when false positives hurt (spam filters).
- **recall** — Of real items, how many were caught; the metric when false negatives hurt (fraud, disease screening).
- **ROC-AUC** — The probability a random positive outranks a random negative, across thresholds; PR curves are more informative for imbalanced data.
- **ablation** — Removing a feature or component and measuring the drop; credit assignment that proves a feature earns its keep.
- **feature engineering judgment** — Knowing which transforms encode real signal vs noise-fitting, validated by ablations, watched for leakage: 'a feature is a hypothesis — I test it like one.'

Sources for this module:
- **scikit-learn Documentation** (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) — User guide and API reference: the classical-ML vocabulary interviewers expect.
- **Google Machine Learning Crash Course** (https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course) — Free applied ML course: framing, training, and generalization, with exercises.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
The modeling vocabulary DS interviews assume: which model for which problem, how you validate it, and which metric matches the cost.

The modeling drill: every exercise starts from the decision the prediction serves, not from the algorithm. Frame first, baseline second, validate honestly — and explain the model choice aloud as if a stakeholder asked 'why this one?'
1. Frame the problem: what is predicted, for whom, at what moment, and what does an error cost? The metric follows the cost.
2. Establish the baseline: a simple model (or heuristic) whose performance every fancier model must beat to justify its complexity.
3. Split with discipline: train for fitting, validation for selection, test touched once at the end. Say the split strategy aloud.
4. Choose the metric from the error costs: precision where false positives hurt, recall where misses hurt, ROC-AUC/PR for ranking quality.
5. Validate honestly: cross-validation where data is small, learning curves to diagnose bias vs variance, ablations to credit features.
6. Explain the choice aloud: decision → alternatives considered → why this one → what would change your mind.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Build a model-selection case study on a classification dataset: frame the business decision, derive the metric from error costs, establish a baseline, compare three model families with cross-validated evaluation, run ablations on your engineered features, and document the final choice with the alternatives-rejected reasoning. Deliver the notebook plus a one-page memo: the recommendation, the evidence, the risks. The memo is the interview artifact.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Preparation, not a credential: this module confers no certificate and makes no placement claims. Model selection here is interview-scale; production modeling adds data pipelines, monitoring, and stakeholder constraints this module doesn't simulate. Metrics are taught as decision tools, not as leaderboard targets.

cards.front: Why is randomization ‘the whole game’ in experiments?
cards.back: Random assignment balances confounders — known and unknown — across arms, making the difference in outcomes attributable to the treatment. Without it, you’re comparing different populations and calling it an effect.

cards.front: What is a novelty effect, and how do you handle it?
cards.back: Users engage with the new thing because it's new, not because it's better — the early lift fades. Guard by running long enough for behavior to stabilize and by checking the lift's time trend. The interview line: 'Novelty is the first lie every test tells; I run past the curiosity phase.'

cards.front: How do you read experiment results honestly?
cards.back: Check the primary metric’s confidence interval (not just the point estimate), verify guardrail metrics didn’t regress, look for heterogeneous effects across segments, and confirm the result survives the pre-registered analysis. The interview line: ‘I report what the data says, including the inconvenient parts.’

cards.front: Why is peeking at A/B results a sin?
cards.back: Every peek is another chance for noise to look significant — the false-positive rate compounds with each look. Fixes: pre-commit to runtime from power analysis, or use sequential methods designed for interim looks. The interview line: ‘decide the stopping rule before the test starts.’

cards.front: When do you NOT A/B test?
cards.back: When you can’t randomize cleanly (network effects, tiny samples), when the effect needs months to matter, when it’s unethical, or when the answer is obvious from data. Alternatives: quasi-experiments (diff-in-diff), holdouts, or just ship with monitoring.

cards.front: What's the interview line for peeking?
cards.back: 'Decide the stopping rule before the test starts': every interim look is another roll of the dice, and significance under repeated testing isn't 5% anymore. Pre-commit to runtime from the power analysis, or use sequential methods designed for interim looks.

cards.front: How do you explain sample ratio mismatch (SRM)?
cards.back: SRM is when the observed split differs from the randomization design — say 52/48 instead of 50/50. It signals a broken mechanism: assignment bugs, filtering that differs by arm, or bots. The line: 'Check the split before the result; a broken randomization invalidates everything downstream.'

cards.front: What do you say about sequential testing and always-valid p-values?
cards.back: Peeking breaks fixed-horizon math, so either pre-commit to a sample size or use sequential methods with alpha spending — methods that price each interim look. The honest line: 'If the business must peek, I pay for it with sequential testing; free peeking is just p-hacking with extra steps.'

cards.front: Pre-registering the analysis plan prevents:
cards.back: **HARKing — hypothesizing after results are known, and metric cherry-picking** — Decisions made after seeing data are rationalizations; pre-registration keeps the test honest. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Network effects (users influencing each other) break A/B tests because:
cards.back: **Treatment leaks into control — randomization’s promise broken** — Randomization assumes independent units; interference between users contaminates both arms. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Peeking inflates false positives because:
cards.back: **Each interim look is another roll of the dice — significance under repeated testing isn’t 5% anymore** — Multiple comparisons: with enough looks, noise will eventually cross the threshold. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: A significant primary metric with regressed guardrail metrics means:
cards.back: **The win has a cost — investigate the tradeoff before deciding** — Guardrails exist to catch wins that break something else; net impact decides. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **randomization** — Random assignment to treatment/control; balances confounders known and unknown, making outcome differences attributable to the treatment — 'the whole game.'
- **treatment / control** — The changed experience vs the baseline; the comparison that isolates the causal effect.
- **power** — The probability of detecting a real effect of a given size; the complement of the Type II error rate.
- **minimum detectable effect (MDE)** — The smallest lift worth detecting; smaller MDEs need larger samples — sizing starts here.
- **sample size** — Determined by power, significance level, baseline variance, and MDE before the test starts; 'decide the stopping rule before the test starts.'
- **primary metric** — The one pre-registered success measure; read via its confidence interval, not just the point estimate.
- **guardrail metrics** — Secondary metrics that must not regress; they catch wins that break something else.
- **peeking** — Checking results mid-test and stopping on significance; each look compounds the false-positive rate — a sin without sequential methods.
- **multiple testing** — Testing many metrics/variants inflates false positives; corrections (Bonferroni and friends) or pre-registered primaries control it.
- **HARKing** — Hypothesizing after results are known; pre-registration of the analysis plan is the defense.
- **network effects / interference** — Users influencing each other breaks randomization's promise: treatment leaks into control.
- **heterogeneous treatment effects** — The effect differs across segments; the average can hide that a change helps some users and harms others.
- **quasi-experiment** — Causal inference without randomization (diff-in-diff, regression discontinuity); the fallback when A/B testing is impossible or unethical.

Sources for this module:
- **Evan Miller: A/B Testing** (https://www.evanmiller.org/ab-testing/) — The long-standing practitioner's guide to designing and reading randomized experiments.
- **A leading free learning platform: Statistics & Probability** (https://www.khanacademy.org/math) — Free, rigorous statistics floor: distributions, inference, and hypothesis testing.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Experimentation is the most-tested DS topic at product companies: design the test, size it, read it — and name every way it can lie.

The experiment-design drill: given a product change, produce the full design on a whiteboard in 20 minutes — randomization, metrics, sizing, reading plan, and the pre-mortem of everything that can go wrong. Interviewers grade the sins you name unprompted.
1. State the hypothesis and the decision the test informs; name what would change your mind.
2. Define the randomization unit (user, session, cluster) and check for interference — network effects kill user-level randomization.
3. Choose the primary metric before anything else, plus guardrails; pre-register the analysis plan to block HARKing and metric shopping.
4. Size the test: MDE from business relevance, then sample size and runtime from power analysis. Commit to the runtime — no peeking.
5. Name the sins and their defenses: peeking (fixed horizon or sequential methods), multiple testing (corrections), novelty effects (run long enough).
6. Plan the read: primary metric's confidence interval, guardrail check, segment heterogeneity, and the ship/hold/iterate decision rule.
7. State when you would NOT A/B test: can't randomize cleanly, tiny samples, unethical, or the answer is obvious — and name the quasi-experimental alternative.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Design three experiments for a fictional subscription product: a checkout-flow change, a pricing test, and a recommendation-ranking change with likely network effects. For each, deliver: the hypothesis, randomization unit with interference analysis, primary metric and guardrails, MDE and sample-size reasoning, the pre-registered analysis plan, the sin pre-mortem, and the read/decision rule. Present one as a 20-minute whiteboard talk; the other two as one-page designs. The interviewer will attack the randomization — be ready.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Preparation, not a credential: this module confers no certificate and makes no placement claims. Experiment design here is interview-scale reasoning; real experimentation platforms add sequential testing, variance reduction, and infrastructure this module doesn't simulate. Power-analysis arithmetic is taught conceptually — use proper tooling for real sizing.

notes.title: Worked example: Pre-registering the analysis plan prevents:
notes.body:
**Problem.** Pre-registering the analysis plan prevents:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** HARKing — hypothesizing after results are known, and metric cherry-picking
- **Why:** Decisions made after seeing data are rationalizations; pre-registration keeps the test honest. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Decisions made after seeing data are rationalizations; pre-registration keeps the test honest.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Data interviews test judgment as much as syntax. In Experimentation and A/B Testing, these habits fail candidates:
- **SQL without thinking in sets.** Row-by-row mental models break on real queries. Think in sets, joins, and aggregations — say the grain of every result out loud.
- **No business framing.** A metric without a decision it informs is trivia. Every analysis in Experimentation and A/B Testing starts from: what decision does this change?
- **Experiment sloppiness.** Peeking at results, ignoring power, confusing correlation with lift. Design the test before you look at the data.
- **Pretty charts, no insight.** Visualization is argument, not decoration. Every chart needs a title that states the conclusion, not the topic.
- **Can't walk the pipeline end to end.** Knowing the modeling step but not ingestion, validation, or serving. Interviewers probe the seams — own the whole pipeline.
- **Answering before clarifying.** Ambiguous question, instant query. Ask about grain, time window, definitions, and edge cases first — it mirrors the real job.

choices: Each interim look is another roll of the dice — significance under repeated testing isn’t 5% anymore

quiz.q: Testing 20 metrics at 5% significance without correction means:
choices: You expect about one false positive by chance alone — multiple testing inflates the error rate

quiz.q: Heterogeneous treatment effects matter because:
choices: A positive average can hide harm to a segment — the ship decision needs the segment view

choices: You can't randomize (e.g. a launched feature) but have a comparable control group and pre-period data

cards.front: How do you frame an ambiguous business question?
cards.back: Restate it as a measurable question, choose metrics before touching data (what would change your mind?), then plan the analysis. The interview line: ‘metrics first, data second — otherwise the data picks the question for you.’

cards.front: What goes in an analysis plan, and what are sanity checks?
cards.back: Plan: question, metrics, data sources, methods, caveats — written before touching data. Sanity checks: row counts, distributions, known totals — run first, every time. The interview line: ‘the plan prevents fishing; the checks prevent embarrassment.’

cards.front: How do you build a case-study narrative?
cards.back: Arc: question → approach → key findings (one chart each) → recommendation. Anticipate follow-ups (caveats, alternative explanations) and address the biggest one proactively. The one-page summary: decision, evidence, risks — nothing else.

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Framing an ambiguous business question'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: For 'Choosing metrics before touching data', what’s the tradeoff question you should answer before the interviewer asks it?
cards.back: Every technique has a cost: name what you gain, what you pay, and when you’d choose the alternative. ‘It depends’ is only a good answer when you then explain what it depends on.

cards.front: What's the interview line for case framing?
cards.back: 'Metrics first, data second — otherwise the data picks the question for you.' Restate the ambiguous prompt as a measurable question, choose what would change your mind, then touch the data. The plan prevents fishing; the sanity checks prevent embarrassment.

cards.front: How do you discuss metric choice in a case study?
cards.back: Tie the metric to the business lever: a marketplace optimizes matches per session, a subscription optimizes retention cohorts, a marketplace optimizes conversion. Say which moves first (leading indicator) and what confirms it (lagging outcome), plus one guardrail. The line: 'I name the north star, the input I move, and the guardrail I won't break.'

cards.front: What does 'sizing an opportunity' look like in a case?
cards.back: Multiply: affected population × baseline rate × plausible lift × value per unit. Keep the math on one line and sanity-check against known totals. Precision is fake; the order of magnitude is the point. The line: 'Rough and checked beats precise and wrong — I size to the nearest order of magnitude.'

cards.front: Addressing the biggest objection proactively is strong because:

cards.front: Sanity checks come before analysis because:
cards.back: **Garbage in, garbage out — validating the data’s shape first saves the whole analysis** — An analysis on broken data is worse than no analysis — it’s confidently wrong. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Choosing metrics before touching data prevents:

notes.body:
A full case walked end to end: ambiguous prompt, metric choice, analysis, and the story — the format product DS interviews use.

The case drill: 45 minutes from ambiguous prompt to one-page summary, narrated throughout. The discipline is sequence — frame, plan, check, analyze, narrate — never analysis before framing.
1. Restate the ambiguous prompt as a measurable question; confirm the decision it informs before proceeding.

5. Analyze in the planned order; when the data surprises you, update the plan explicitly — no silent fishing.
6. Build the narrative arc: one chart per key finding, each earning its place toward the recommendation.
7. Anticipate the biggest follow-up and address it proactively; write the one-page summary: decision, evidence, risks.

cards.front: How do you handle DS mock rounds (stats, live analysis, experiment design, model choice)?
cards.back: Stats: definitions with the intuition, then the caveat. Live analysis: narrate EDA as you go (distributions, then relationships, then quality). Experiment design: the full checklist aloud. Model choice: decision with alternatives. The interview line: ‘each round has a shape — I rehearse the shape.’

cards.front: How do you tell the failed-analysis story?
cards.back: Own the miss early, name what was wrong and what it cost, then the concrete process change with evidence it stuck. The interview line: ‘the failure is the setup; the changed practice is the point.’

cards.front: What does a scored review and redrill plan look like?
cards.back: Score each round against a rubric (correctness, complexity stated, communication, time), list misses, and convert each miss into a dated redrill task. The plan is specific: ‘three sliding-window problems, timed, by Thursday’ — not ‘practice more.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Timed stats and probability rounds'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: For 'Live analysis screens', what’s the tradeoff question you should answer before the interviewer asks it?
cards.back: Every technique has a cost: name what you gain, what you pay, and when you’d choose the alternative. ‘It depends’ is only a good answer when you then explain what it depends on.

cards.front: What are the four DS round shapes?
cards.back: Stats (definition → intuition → caveat → computation), live analysis (narrated EDA in order), experiment design (full checklist aloud, sins unprompted), model choice (decision with alternatives). 'Each round has a shape — I rehearse the shape.'

cards.front: How do you open a live-analysis screen?
cards.back: Narrate the plan before touching data: restate the question, list the two or three checks that decide the answer, then run them in that order. Examiners grade structure more than speed. The line: 'I say what I'm about to do before I do it — the plan is half the grade.'

cards.front: What do you do when your analysis contradicts the business request?
cards.back: Report the honest result with the evidence, quantify the size of the contradiction, and propose what it suggests instead — then let them decide. Hiding an inconvenient answer is a career-ender. The line: 'The data said no; my job is to make the no useful.'

cards.front: A redrill plan is effective when it is:

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **mock circuit (DS)** — Timed simulations across the four DS round types: stats, coding/analysis, experimentation, case — each with its own shape and rubric.
- **stats round shape** — Definitions with intuition, then the caveat, then a tiny computation; precision under time.
- **live analysis shape** — Narrated EDA: distributions, then relationships, then quality; the interviewer scores investigative method.
- **experiment-design shape** — The full checklist aloud: randomization, metrics, sizing, sins, read plan; sins named unprompted score highest.
- **model-choice shape** — Decision with alternatives: framing, baseline, metric from costs, honest validation.
- **failed-analysis story** — The behavioral artifact: own the miss early, name the cost, show the concrete process change with evidence it stuck — 'the failure is the setup; the changed practice is the point.'
- **scored review** — Rubric scoring per round immediately after: correctness, complexity stated, communication, time.
- **redrill plan** — Each miss converted to a specific, dated task; 'three power-analysis problems by Thursday' — not 'practice more.'

Sources for this module:
- **DataLemur** (https://datalemur.com) — SQL and data interview questions in the style real screens ask them; used for timed reps, not answers.
- **scikit-learn Documentation** (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) — User guide and API reference: the classical-ML vocabulary interviewers expect.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Full simulations across the four DS round types — stats, coding, experimentation, and case — scored against rubrics.

The DS mock protocol: one full loop per session, real timing, narration mandatory. Rotate the weak round to the front — you train the miss, not the strength.
1. Assemble the loop: 15-min stats round, 20-min live analysis screen, 20-min experiment whiteboard, 15-min model-choice deep dive, 10-min failed-analysis story.
2. Run stats with the shape: definition, intuition, caveat, tiny computation — say the caveat before they ask.
3. Run live analysis narrated: distributions, relationships, quality checks — in that order, out loud.
4. Run experiment design with the full checklist aloud; name the sins (peeking, interference, novelty) unprompted.
5. Run model choice as decision-with-alternatives: framing, baseline, metric from error costs, validation discipline.
6. Tell the failed-analysis story: own the miss early, the cost, the process change, the evidence it stuck.
7. Score every round against the rubric immediately; convert each miss to a dated redrill task before the next loop.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Run and document three full DS mock loops over two weeks. Per loop, deliver: the prompts used for each of the five rounds, rubric scores with verbatim misses, the redrill plan with dates, and a trend summary of which miss categories shrink. Final deliverable: a readiness self-assessment naming your strongest round shape, your costliest remaining miss category, and the dated plan to close it.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Preparation, not a credential: this module confers no certificate and makes no placement claims. Mocks simulate the four round shapes; real loops vary by company and interviewer, and team fit is scored beyond any rubric. Scores measure performance on the day — aim redrills with them, don't predict outcomes with them.

notes.title: Worked example: A redrill plan is effective when it is:
notes.body:
**Problem.** A redrill plan is effective when it is:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Specific, dated, and tied to named misses from the scored review
- **Why:** Specificity turns review into training; vague plans evaporate. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Specificity turns review into training; vague plans evaporate.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Data interviews test judgment as much as syntax. In Data Science Mock Circuit, these habits fail candidates:
- **SQL without thinking in sets.** Row-by-row mental models break on real queries. Think in sets, joins, and aggregations — say the grain of every result out loud.
- **No business framing.** A metric without a decision it informs is trivia. Every analysis in Data Science Mock Circuit starts from: what decision does this change?
- **Experiment sloppiness.** Peeking at results, ignoring power, confusing correlation with lift. Design the test before you look at the data.
- **Pretty charts, no insight.** Visualization is argument, not decoration. Every chart needs a title that states the conclusion, not the topic.
- **Can't walk the pipeline end to end.** Knowing the modeling step but not ingestion, validation, or serving. Interviewers probe the seams — own the whole pipeline.
- **Answering before clarifying.** Ambiguous question, instant query. Ask about grain, time window, definitions, and edge cases first — it mirrors the real job.

cards.front: What’s the logical order of a SQL query — and why does it matter?
cards.back: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY: the written order isn’t the execution order. It matters because aliases defined in SELECT aren’t visible in WHERE, and window functions come after WHERE — the interview line: ‘I write in SELECT order but think in execution order.’

cards.front: Inner vs left join — when does each lie?
cards.back: Inner drops non-matching rows from both sides (silently shrinking your denominator). Left keeps all left rows with NULLs for misses. The lie: inner-joining then counting ‘all users’ — you’ve excluded the unmatched. State which side must survive.

cards.front: What do GROUP BY mistakes look like in interviews?
cards.back: Selecting non-aggregated columns not in the GROUP BY (invalid or arbitrary), filtering groups in WHERE instead of HAVING, and wrong grain (grouping by day when the question wants per user). The interview line: ‘every SELECT column is either grouped or aggregated — no exceptions.’

cards.front: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)?
cards.back: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values in that column. The interview trap: ‘how many users?’ with nullable columns — pick the wrong one and your metric is silently off.

cards.front: When do you use EXISTS vs a JOIN?
cards.back: EXISTS for semi-join questions (‘customers WITH orders’) — it stops at the first match and never fans out. JOIN when you need columns from the other table. The interview line: ‘EXISTS asks a yes/no question; JOIN brings back data.’

cards.front: What's the interview line for join choice?
cards.back: 'State which side must survive': inner joins silently drop non-matches and shrink your denominator — if you're counting 'all users,' the users table must survive the join. The join type is a business decision, not a syntax choice.

cards.front: How do you debug a query that returns wrong numbers?
cards.back: Four checks in order: row counts at each join (fan-out doubles aggregates), the grain (what does one row mean?), the filter (WHERE vs HAVING on aggregates), and NULLs (they silently drop rows in joins). The line: 'Wrong numbers are almost always grain or fan-out — I check the row count first.'

cards.front: What do you say about NULLs in joins and aggregations?
cards.back: NULL never equals NULL, so joins drop them; COUNT(column) skips them while COUNT(*) doesn't; aggregates like SUM ignore them. In interviews, name the NULL policy for the key columns before writing the query. The line: 'I state my NULL assumptions out loud before the query, not after the bug.'

cards.front: NOT IN is dangerous with NULLs because:
cards.back: **A single NULL in the subquery makes the whole predicate UNKNOWN — zero rows returned** — NULL semantics: NOT IN with a NULL never evaluates true; NOT EXISTS doesn’t have this trap. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: EXISTS is preferred over IN for ‘has at least one’ because:
cards.back: **It short-circuits on first match and is NULL-safe** — Correlated EXISTS stops scanning at the first hit; IN materializes the whole set. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: COUNT(email) < COUNT(*) means:
cards.back: **Some rows have NULL email — COUNT(column) skips NULLs** — COUNT(column) excludes NULLs; COUNT(*) counts every row regardless. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Filtering on SUM(revenue) > 1000 belongs in:
cards.back: **HAVING — it filters groups after aggregation** — WHERE filters rows pre-aggregation; HAVING filters the grouped results. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **logical query order** — FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → window functions → ORDER BY: 'I write in SELECT order but think in execution order.'
- **inner join** — Keeps only matching rows from both sides; silently shrinks denominators when matches are missing.
- **left join** — Keeps all left rows, NULLs for misses; the safe default when the left side must survive.
- **GROUP BY grain** — The grouping columns define the answer's unit; wrong grain, wrong answer — 'every SELECT column is either grouped or aggregated.'
- **HAVING** — Filters groups after aggregation; aggregate conditions in WHERE are always wrong.
- **COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)** — COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values — the interview trap behind 'how many users?'
- **subquery** — A query nested inside another; uncorrelated runs once, correlated runs per outer row.
- **EXISTS (semi-join)** — 'Has at least one': stops at the first match, never fans out — 'EXISTS asks a yes/no question; JOIN brings back data.'
- **anti-join** — LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL or NOT EXISTS: the 'what's missing' pattern ('customers with no orders').
- **NOT IN NULL trap** — A single NULL in the subquery makes NOT IN return zero rows; NOT EXISTS has no such trap.
- **orphan rows** — Child rows with no parent (orders with no customer); found with anti-joins, they signal data-quality problems.

Sources for this module:
- **Mode SQL Tutorial** (https://mode.com/sql-tutorial/) — Free interactive SQL tutorial, from basic selects through window functions and analytics patterns.
- **SQLZoo** (https://sqlzoo.net/) — Interactive SQL exercises with immediate feedback; the rep work for joins, subqueries, and aggregation.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Analyst SQL from zero to interview-ready: the query shapes behind 'how many users did X' and the join mistakes that silently wrong-answer them.

The foundations drill: every query is built in the same order — grain, joins, filters, aggregates — and checked against a three-row mental dataset. Speed comes from the routine, not from rushing.
1. Read the question and state the grain: 'one row per user.' Write it as a comment.
2. Choose the join by survival: which side must keep all its rows? Default to LEFT when the counted population must survive.
3. Write FROM and JOINs first, then WHERE (row filters), then GROUP BY, then HAVING (group filters) — execution order, not SELECT order.
4. Check every non-aggregated SELECT column is in the GROUP BY; check every aggregate filter lives in HAVING.
5. For 'has at least one' use EXISTS; for 'has none' use NOT EXISTS — never NOT IN on nullable columns.
6. Verify on a tiny mental dataset: three rows per table, including a NULL and a non-match. Trace the joins by hand.
7. Read the query back as a sentence: does it still answer the asked question at the stated grain?
notes.code:
-- Analyst staple: conversion with the denominator protected
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) * 1.0
       / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT c.customer_id), 0) AS conversion_rate
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;  -- LEFT keeps every customer

-- Anti-join: customers with no orders (NULL-safe)
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);

quiz.explain: GROUP BY defines the answer's unit; a sloppy grain gives a confident wrong answer. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: NULLIF in a division protects against:
choices: Division by zero — NULLIF turns 0 into NULL, yielding NULL instead of an error
quiz.explain: Defensive arithmetic: a zero denominator becomes NULL, not a crashed query. See the 'Hands-on procedure' in this module.

quiz.q: A correlated subquery differs from an uncorrelated one in that it:
choices: References the outer query and executes per outer row
quiz.explain: Correlation ties the inner query to each outer row — EXISTS is the classic case. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: Counting 'all users who ordered' with an INNER JOIN then COUNT(DISTINCT user) is wrong when:
choices: Some users have no orders — inner join silently drops them from the denominator
quiz.explain: The join type decides the population; the count only counts survivors. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: WHERE vs HAVING: the rule is:
choices: WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters groups after
quiz.explain: Logical query order: row filters first, group filters after GROUP BY. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: Orphan orders (no matching customer) are found with:
choices: An anti-join — LEFT JOIN ... WHERE customer_id IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS
quiz.explain: 'What's missing' is the anti-join's job; orphans signal data-quality issues. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

cards.front: What spreadsheet skills do interviewers test?
cards.back: Lookups without footguns (XLOOKUP/INDEX-MATCH over VLOOKUP’s fragility), absolute vs relative references ($), pivot tables for fast exploration, and knowing when the spreadsheet stops being the tool (size, reproducibility → SQL/Python).

cards.front: Absolute vs relative references — the 30-second version?
cards.back: $ locks the reference: $A$1 never moves, A$1 locks the row, $A1 locks the column. The interview line: ‘I lock what shouldn’t move when the formula fills — getting this wrong is the #1 spreadsheet bug.’

cards.front: What are pivot tables for in an interview?
cards.back: Fast exploratory aggregation: drag dimensions to rows/columns, values to aggregation — distributions and cuts in seconds, no formulas. The interview line: ‘pivots are the spreadsheet’s GROUP BY.’

cards.front: What spreadsheet techniques do interviewers probe?
cards.back: Cleaning with formulas (TRIM, TEXTSPLIT, IFERROR — auditable, repeatable), and what-if models (data tables, scenarios, goal seek) for sensitivity analysis. The interview line: ‘formulas over manual edits — the cleaning must be re-runnable.’

cards.front: When does a spreadsheet stop being the right tool?
cards.back: When data outgrows memory/manual steps, when the analysis must be reproducible and auditable, or when it feeds production. The interview line: ‘spreadsheets are for exploration; pipelines are for repetition.’

cards.front: What's the interview line for the spreadsheet-to-SQL handoff?
cards.back: 'Spreadsheets are for exploration; pipelines are for repetition': when steps must be repeated reliably, data outgrows memory, or the analysis must be auditable, the grid stops being the tool. Naming the handoff point is the senior move.

cards.front: How do you discuss data validation in spreadsheets?
cards.back: Three defenses: input validation rules (dropdowns, ranges), conditional formatting that screams when something's off, and a checksum area (totals, row counts) that must reconcile. The line: 'A spreadsheet without checks is a rumor — I build the alarm into the sheet.'

cards.front: What do you say when asked to model a forecast in a sheet?
cards.back: Keep it transparent: show assumptions in their own cells, use scenarios (base/bull/bear) not single numbers, and make every formula traceable back to inputs. The line: 'Forecast cells I can audit; hard-coded numbers I can't defend.'

cards.front: The clearest signal to move from spreadsheet to SQL/Python is:
cards.back: **Manual steps that must be repeated reliably — reproducibility and scale** — Repetition + scale + auditability: the point where manual stops being trustworthy. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Formula-based cleaning beats manual edits because:
cards.back: **It’s auditable and re-runnable — manual edits can’t be verified or repeated** — Repeatability is the difference between analysis and anecdote. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: A pivot table’s ‘values’ field with ‘count’ answers:
cards.back: **How many rows fall in each row/column combination — a cross-tab** — Pivots reshape long data into summary grids: the fastest path to ‘break it down by X.’ Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Copying =A1*B1 down a column should usually become:
cards.back: **=A2*B2 — relative references shift with the row** — Relative references move with the fill; absolute ($) pins them. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **XLOOKUP / INDEX-MATCH** — Modern lookups without VLOOKUP's fragility (column-insert breakage, leftward-lookup limits); the interview-safe lookup family.
- **VLOOKUP footguns** — Breaks on inserted columns, can't look left, exact-match flag forgotten; know why interviewers prefer the alternatives.
- **absolute reference ($)** — $A$1 never moves on fill; A$1 locks the row, $A1 locks the column — 'I lock what shouldn't move when the formula fills.'
- **relative reference** — Shifts with the fill (A1 → A2 down a column); the default, and the #1 spreadsheet bug when misapplied.
- **pivot table** — Drag-to-aggregate exploration: dimensions to rows/columns, values to aggregation — 'the spreadsheet's GROUP BY.'
- **cross-tab** — A pivot's row/column grid of counts or sums; the fastest path to 'break it down by X.'
- **formula-based cleaning** — TRIM, TEXTSPLIT, IFERROR: auditable, re-runnable cleaning — 'formulas over manual edits.'
- **what-if model** — Data tables, scenarios, goal seek: sensitivity analysis showing how outputs move with inputs.
- **reproducibility limit** — The point where manual steps, size, or auditability demand SQL/Python: 'spreadsheets are for exploration; pipelines are for repetition.'

Sources for this module:
- **Google Sheets Help** (https://support.google.com/docs) — Official reference for the spreadsheet half of analyst interviews.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
The spreadsheet half of analyst screens: fast, correct lookup and pivot work — plus knowing when the data has outgrown the grid.

The spreadsheet drill: every exercise is a messy grid and a question, done without touching the raw data by hand. If a step can't be re-run from formulas, it's not done.
1. Freeze the raw data: work on a copy or a new sheet; raw stays untouched and auditable.
2. Clean with formulas only: TRIM whitespace, TEXTSPLIT delimited fields, IFERROR for graceful failures — every edit re-runnable.
3. Lock references deliberately: $ on what shouldn't move when the formula fills; verify by filling and spot-checking.
4. Look up with XLOOKUP/INDEX-MATCH; handle misses explicitly (IFNA) instead of letting #N/A propagate silently.
5. Explore with pivot tables before formulas: drag dimensions, check the cross-tab, then formalize the finding.
6. Build what-if models with data tables/scenarios for sensitivity questions; document the assumptions in cells, not in your head.
7. State the handoff point: when the data outgrows the grid (size, repetition, auditability), name SQL/Python as the next tool and why.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Deliver a spreadsheet case: a messy 10k-row sales extract and five stakeholder questions (lookup-heavy, pivot-heavy, and one what-if). The workbook must contain: untouched raw data, formula-only cleaning layers, correct absolute/relative references throughout, pivot explorations, a what-if scenario table, and a 'handoff memo' naming which question outgrows the grid and why. Every formula auditable; no manual edits anywhere.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Preparation, not a credential: this module confers no certificate and makes no placement claims. Spreadsheet mechanics are stable skills, but UI details vary across tools and versions — the concepts (references, pivots, reproducibility) transfer; the clicks may differ. Interviewers test judgment about tool limits as much as formula speed.

notes.title: Worked example: The clearest signal to move from spreadsheet to SQL/Python is:
notes.body:
**Problem.** The clearest signal to move from spreadsheet to SQL/Python is:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Manual steps that must be repeated reliably — reproducibility and scale
- **Why:** Repetition + scale + auditability: the point where manual stops being trustworthy. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Repetition + scale + auditability: the point where manual stops being trustworthy.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Data interviews test judgment as much as syntax. In Spreadsheets and Modeling, these habits fail candidates:
- **SQL without thinking in sets.** Row-by-row mental models break on real queries. Think in sets, joins, and aggregations — say the grain of every result out loud.
- **No business framing.** A metric without a decision it informs is trivia. Every analysis in Spreadsheets and Modeling starts from: what decision does this change?
- **Experiment sloppiness.** Peeking at results, ignoring power, confusing correlation with lift. Design the test before you look at the data.
- **Pretty charts, no insight.** Visualization is argument, not decoration. Every chart needs a title that states the conclusion, not the topic.
- **Can't walk the pipeline end to end.** Knowing the modeling step but not ingestion, validation, or serving. Interviewers probe the seams — own the whole pipeline.
- **Answering before clarifying.** Ambiguous question, instant query. Ask about grain, time window, definitions, and edge cases first — it mirrors the real job.

cards.front: How do you choose the right chart?
cards.back: Match chart to question: trends → line, comparisons → bar, composition → stacked bar (not pie for many slices), distributions → histogram, relationships → scatter. The interview trap: the truncated y-axis — always check whether the axis starts at zero before concluding.

cards.front: What’s the truncated-bar trap?
cards.back: A y-axis not starting at zero visually magnifies tiny differences — honest or sloppy, it misleads. The interview line: ‘I check the axis before I believe the chart — including my own.’

cards.front: What makes a dashboard that ‘answers questions’?
cards.back: Golden signals up top, drill-down from symptom to cause, time-range comparisons, and annotations for deploys — organized by the questions on-call asks at 3am, not by data source. The interview line: ‘a dashboard is a UI for incident questions.’

cards.front: What’s the insight → action → recommendation arc?
cards.back: Insight (what the data says), implication (why it matters to the business), recommendation (what to do, with expected impact). Data without a recommendation is trivia; the arc turns analysis into decisions.

cards.front: How do you present to non-technical stakeholders?
cards.back: Lead with the recommendation, then the one chart that proves it; plain language, no jargon; name caveats briefly and honestly; end with the decision you need. The interview line: ‘I present conclusions, not queries.’

cards.front: What's the interview line for chart critique?
cards.back: 'What question is it answering — and does the visual actually answer it?' Ask it of every chart, including your own, before you ask anything about prettiness. A beautiful chart answering the wrong question is worse than no chart.

cards.front: How do you critique a pie chart in an interview?
cards.back: Name the real issue: humans compare angles poorly — bar charts beat pies for more than two or three slices. But be diplomatic: acknowledge when a pie works (one part-of-whole message, few categories). The line: 'I judge the chart by the question it answers, not the chart type — but pies get scrutinized.'

cards.front: What do you say about color and accessibility in charts?
cards.back: Two rules: never let color be the only encoding (add labels or patterns for colorblind viewers), and use color to guide the eye — highlight the insight, gray out the rest. The line: 'Color is a highlighter, not the message — the chart must survive black-and-white.'

cards.front: The first critique question for any chart is:
cards.back: **What question is it answering — and does the visual actually answer it** — A beautiful chart answering the wrong question is worse than no chart. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Leading with the recommendation works because:
cards.back: **Executives decide — the supporting evidence follows the decision they need to make** — BLUF (bottom line up front): busy stakeholders need the ask before the analysis. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: An analysis without a recommendation is weak because:
cards.back: **Stakeholders need decisions, not trivia — the arc connects data to action** — The job is driving decisions; insight and implication earn the right to recommend. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Deploy annotations on dashboards help because:
cards.back: **They correlate behavior changes with releases — the first suspect in any regression** — ‘What changed?’ is the first incident question; annotations answer it at a glance. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Charts as arguments: picking the right visual, keeping it honest, and turning a dashboard into a recommendation.

The visualization drill: every exercise hands you a dataset and a stakeholder question; you produce exactly one chart and a three-sentence arc. Constraint breeds clarity — the interviewer sees whether you can choose.
1. Write the question the chart must answer in one sentence before opening any tool.
2. Choose the visual from the question type (trend/comparison/composition/distribution/relationship) — defend the choice in one line.
3. Build it with honest scales: check the axis starts where it should; annotate context (deploys, events) that changes interpretation.
4. Critique it as an adversary: what question does it actually answer? What could a viewer wrongly conclude?
5. Write the arc: insight (what the data says), implication (why it matters), recommendation (what to do, expected impact).
6. Present BLUF: recommendation first, then the one proving chart, caveats briefly, end with the decision you need.
7. For dashboards: organize by the questions asked at 3am (symptom → cause), not by data source; every view must drive a decision.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Deliver a stakeholder deck for a product metric deep-dive: five charts max, each with a stated question, an honest axis, and a place in the insight → implication → recommendation arc. Include one deliberately-bad chart you then critique and fix (truncated axis or wrong visual), and a one-page dashboard spec organized by incident questions. Present it in 10 minutes, BLUF-first, ending with the decision you're asking for.

cards.front: How do you explain a north-star metric versus input metrics?
cards.back: The north star is the single number that captures value delivered (e.g., nights booked for a travel site); input metrics are the levers teams move (search conversion, listing quality). North star for alignment, inputs for action. The line: 'North star for where we're going, inputs for what I do Monday morning.'

cards.front: How do you analyze a funnel?
cards.back: Step-by-step conversion with drop-off at each stage, segmented (device, cohort, channel) because aggregate funnels hide the story. The interview move: name the biggest absolute drop first — that’s where the leverage is.

cards.front: Cohorts and retention curves — the interview version?
cards.back: Group users by start period (cohort), track retention over time since start: the curve’s shape reveals product health (flattening = sticky, decaying to zero = leaky bucket). Compare cohorts to measure whether changes actually improved retention.

cards.front: Why segment before concluding?
cards.back: Aggregates lie (Simpson’s paradox): the overall trend can reverse within segments. The interview line: ‘I never trust an aggregate until I’ve cut it three ways.’

cards.front: How do you read an experiment result honestly?
cards.back: Primary metric’s confidence interval (not just the point), guardrails for regressions, segment heterogeneity, and whether the result survives the pre-registered analysis. The interview line: ‘I report what the data says, including the inconvenient parts.’

cards.front: What's the interview line for a moved metric?
cards.back: 'Data quality first, segments second, theories last': half of all metric moves are measurement artifacts — instrumentation, pipeline, definitions — so you rule those out before theorizing. Then you cut three ways, because aggregates lie.

cards.front: What do you say about vanity metrics versus actionable metrics?
cards.back: Vanity metrics feel good and move nothing (total signups); actionable metrics tie to a decision (activated users by cohort, with a lever attached). The test: 'if this moves, what would I do differently?' The line: 'Every metric I report carries a decision, or it doesn't make the slide.'

cards.front: How do you discuss seasonality versus a real trend change?
cards.back: Overlay year-over-year comparisons, decompose the series (trend, seasonal, residual), and check whether the change persists after the seasonal adjustment. The line: 'Seasonality is the first suspect; I de-season before I declare a trend.'

cards.front: The FIRST step when a metric moves unexpectedly is:
cards.back: **Verify data quality — instrumentation, pipeline, definitions** — Half of all ‘metric moves’ are measurement artifacts; rule those out before theorizing. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: A significant primary metric with regressed guardrails means:
cards.back: **The win has a cost — investigate the tradeoff before deciding** — Guardrails exist to catch wins that break something else; net impact decides. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Simpson’s paradox warns that:
cards.back: **An aggregate trend can reverse within subgroups — always check segments** — A treatment can look better overall yet worse in every segment — composition effects deceive. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: A retention curve flattening above zero indicates:
cards.back: **A sticky core of users who stay — product-market fit signal** — Flattening means a fraction never leaves; decaying to zero means everyone eventually churns. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **North Star metric** — The single metric capturing core product value; everything else ladders up to it.
- **input metrics** — The levers that move the North Star (acquisition, activation, retention drivers); what teams actually operate day to day.
- **funnel** — Step-by-step conversion with drop-off at each stage; analyze segmented, because aggregate funnels hide the story — 'name the biggest absolute drop first.'
- **cohort** — Users grouped by start period; tracked over time-since-start so product changes are measured against comparable groups.
- **retention curve** — Cohort retention over time: flattening above zero signals a sticky core (product-market fit); decaying to zero is a leaky bucket.
- **segmentation** — Cutting metrics by device, channel, cohort, segment before concluding; 'aggregates lie' — Simpson's paradox lives here.
- **Simpson's paradox** — An aggregate trend reversing within subgroups; the reason you 'never trust an aggregate until you've cut it three ways.'
- **metric-moved drill** — The diagnostic sequence: verify data quality first (instrumentation, pipeline, definitions), then segment, then theorize — 'half of all metric moves are measurement artifacts.'
- **guardrail metrics** — Must-not-regress companions to the primary metric; read with confidence intervals, not point estimates.

Sources for this module:
- **Google Analytics Help** (https://support.google.com/analytics) — Official reference for funnels, cohorts, and the metrics language analysts speak.
- **Evan Miller: A/B Testing** (https://www.evanmiller.org/ab-testing/) — The long-standing practitioner's guide to designing and reading randomized experiments.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
The judgment layer: defining the right metric, slicing it before trusting it, and diagnosing a movement like a detective.

The metrics drill: every exercise is a moved metric or a vague 'define success' prompt. The routine is always data-quality first, segments second, theories last — in that order, every time.
1. Define the metric precisely: numerator, denominator, grain, time window — ambiguity here corrupts everything downstream.
2. Name the North Star it ladders to and the input metrics that move it; check the metric actually measures the decision.
3. When a metric moves: verify data quality FIRST — instrumentation changes, pipeline delays, definition edits — before any product theory.
4. Segment three ways (cohort, channel/device, segment): find where the move lives; aggregates lie.
5. For funnels: compute step-by-step conversion, name the biggest absolute drop — that's the leverage point.
6. For retention: build the cohort curve, compare across cohorts — flattening vs decaying tells you product health.
7. Read experiment results honestly: primary metric's interval, guardrails for regressions, segment heterogeneity — then decide.

Present the diagnoses as 10-minute detective stories ending in a recommendation.

cards.front: How do you run a guided analyst project?
cards.back: Pick a question worth answering (decision attached), get and clean the data with auditable steps, explore with a plan, build the dashboard or deck around the insight-action arc, and write the recommendation memo anticipating pushback. The interview line: ‘every step serves the decision.’

cards.front: How do you make exploratory testing rigorous?
cards.back: Charters: time-boxed missions with a goal (‘explore checkout with invalid inputs for 45 minutes’), session notes, and debriefs. It’s skilled investigation, not random clicking — the charter makes it repeatable and reportable.

cards.front: How do you scope an analyst project so it finishes?
cards.back: One question, one dataset, one decision it informs — written down before touching the data. Cut scope by narrowing the question, never by lowering the bar. The line: 'I scope until I can finish it in the time I have, then I commit to that scope.'

cards.front: How do you handle stakeholder disagreement?
cards.back: Listen for the real objection (often a different question than asked), show your work and caveats honestly, propose the test that would resolve it — and disagree-and-commit cleanly when the decision goes the other way. The interview line: ‘I argue with data, then commit like an owner.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Picking a question worth answering'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: What makes an analyst project portfolio-worthy?
cards.back: A decision-attached question, auditably cleaned data, exploration with a plan, a deliverable on the insight arc, a one-page memo — and a walkthrough that owns the caveats. 'Every step serves the decision': that's what interviewers are checking.

cards.front: What makes documentation of an analyst project strong?
cards.back: Four things: the question and why it matters, data sources with caveats, the analysis steps someone could rerun, and assumptions with their impact if wrong. The line: 'Documentation is how the analysis survives me — question, data, steps, caveats.'

cards.front: How do you discuss stakeholder feedback changing your analysis mid-project?
cards.back: Frame it as analysis doing its job: the feedback revealed a missed assumption, you re-scoped, and the answer got better. Name what changed and what the revision taught you — interviewers love a story where challenge improved rigor. The line: 'Feedback didn't break my analysis; it finished it.'

cards.front: When a stakeholder rejects your analysis, the strongest first move is:
cards.back: **Understand their objection — it’s often a different question than you answered** — Most ‘disagreements’ are misaligned questions; diagnosing the real one resolves them. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: useCallback’s purpose is:
cards.back: **Preserving function identity across renders so memoized children don’t re-render** — A new function identity each render defeats memo on children; useCallback stabilizes it. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: An exploratory testing charter provides:
cards.back: **A time-boxed mission and focus — making exploration deliberate and reportable** — Charters bound the session with purpose; notes and debriefs turn findings into artifacts. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Attaching a decision to the question upfront matters because:
cards.back: **It scopes the analysis — you know when you have enough to recommend** — Decision-less analysis expands forever; a target decision bounds the work. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **question worth answering** — A question with a decision attached; 'decision-less analysis expands forever; a target decision bounds the work.'
- **auditable cleaning** — Every cleaning step re-runnable and reasoned (formulas, code, logged decisions) — never silent manual edits.
- **exploration with a plan** — Time-boxed, question-driven EDA; the plan prevents fishing, the sanity checks prevent embarrassment.
- **insight → action → recommendation** — The arc every deliverable follows: what the data says, why it matters, what to do.
- **recommendation memo** — Decision, evidence, risks — the written artifact stakeholders actually act on.
- **stakeholder pushback** — The expected objections, diagnosed early ('often a different question than you answered') and addressed with data; 'I argue with data, then commit like an owner.'
- **dashboard vs deck** — Dashboards monitor recurring questions; decks argue a specific decision — choose by the job.
- **portfolio narrative** — The 10-minute walkthrough: question → approach → findings → recommendation, with caveats owned proactively.
