cards.front: What’s the 15-minute SQL screen playbook?
cards.back: Clarify the grain and edge cases (1 min), sketch the CTE stages aloud (2 min), write it in passes (core logic → edge cases), sanity-check with a tiny mental dataset, and narrate throughout. If stuck: say what you’d try next — interviewers score the recovery.

cards.front: How do you recover from a wrong first attempt in a live SQL round?
cards.back: Name what’s wrong out loud (‘this double-counts because…’), fix the specific issue (grain, join type, filter placement), and re-verify with the mental dataset. The interview line: ‘recovery is a skill — I show it instead of freezing.’

cards.front: What does a scored review and redrill plan look like?
cards.back: Score each round against a rubric (correctness, complexity stated, communication, time), list misses, and convert each miss into a dated redrill task. The plan is specific: ‘three sliding-window problems, timed, by Thursday’ — not ‘practice more.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Timed mixed-pattern circuits'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: For 'Explaining your query aloud', what’s the tradeoff question you should answer before the interviewer asks it?
cards.back: Every technique has a cost: name what you gain, what you pay, and when you’d choose the alternative. ‘It depends’ is only a good answer when you then explain what it depends on.

cards.front: What's the circuit line for getting stuck?
cards.back: Say what you'd try next and why — out loud. Freezing scores zero on recovery; a named hypothesis ('the grain is probably per session, let me re-verify') shows the method surviving contact with difficulty. Recovery is a skill you demonstrate, not a secret you hide.

cards.front: How do you drill time-boxed pattern recognition?
cards.back: Give yourself 90 seconds per prompt: name the pattern (top-N, gaps-and-islands, funnel), sketch the clause order on paper, then write. Score pattern-first, syntax-second. The drill line: 'Pattern in the first minute; the query is just transcription.'

cards.front: What's the circuit line for explaining before querying?
cards.back: Say the plan in two sentences — what the grain is, which pattern you're using — before writing a single clause. Interviewers grade thinking, and it buys you recovery time when the syntax wobbles. The drill line: 'Explain the grain and the pattern first; the query writes itself.'

cards.front: A redrill plan is effective when it is:
cards.back: **Specific, dated, and tied to named misses from the scored review** — Specificity turns review into training; vague plans evaporate. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Saying the bug out loud before fixing it is strong because:
cards.back: **It proves you diagnose before patching — and lets the interviewer follow** — Diagnose-then-fix beats flailing; narration turns the fix into evidence of method. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: Narrating during a SQL screen helps because:
cards.back: **The interviewer scores your decomposition and recovery, not just the final query** — Live coding is graded on method; narration exposes the thinking being graded. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

cards.front: You’re asked about 'Timed mixed-pattern circuits' and your memory blanks. What’s the strongest recovery?
cards.back: **State what you do know precisely, name the boundary, and reason from first principles aloud** — Interviewers score honesty + reasoning: a precise partial answer with clear boundaries beats a confident fabrication every time. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Full timed circuits mixing every pattern: speed, narration, and recovery — the closest thing to the real screen without one.

The circuit protocol: full mixed sets under the real clock, no pausing, narration mandatory. One circuit per session, scored immediately, redrills scheduled before the next.
1. Assemble a 60-minute circuit: 4 mixed problems (join, window, CTE, analytics pattern) at 15 minutes each.
2. Run each with the playbook: grain, stages aloud, passes, mental-dataset verification, continuous narration.
3. When stuck: say what you'd try next and why — scored recovery beats silent freezing.
4. Read hints as direction: restate the nudge ('so the grain should be per session...') and adjust visibly.
5. Score immediately per the rubric: correctness, recognition speed, narration, recovery, time — misses verbatim.
6. Log every miss into your weak-pattern list; convert each to a dated redrill task before the next circuit.
7. Track the trend across circuits: which patterns stopped costing you time, which still do — train the remainder.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Run and document six full mixed circuits over three weeks. Per circuit deliver: the four problems used, per-problem rubric scores with verbatim misses, the updated weak-pattern list, and the dated redrill plan. Close with a readiness report: recognition-speed trend per pattern family, your recovery highlight reel (best in-round save), and the one pattern still costing you points with its kill plan. This is the training log you review the week of interviews.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Preparation, not a credential: this module confers no certificate and makes no placement claims. Circuits simulate screen pressure; they can't replicate a specific interviewer's style or a company's data. Scores measure training progress on the day — aim redrills with them, don't predict offers with them.

notes.title: Worked example: A redrill plan is effective when it is:
notes.body:
**Problem.** A redrill plan is effective when it is:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Specific, dated, and tied to named misses from the scored review
- **Why:** Specificity turns review into training; vague plans evaporate. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Specificity turns review into training; vague plans evaporate.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Data interviews test judgment as much as syntax. In Drill Circuit Finale, these habits fail candidates:
- **SQL without thinking in sets.** Row-by-row mental models break on real queries. Think in sets, joins, and aggregations — say the grain of every result out loud.
- **No business framing.** A metric without a decision it informs is trivia. Every analysis in Drill Circuit Finale starts from: what decision does this change?
- **Experiment sloppiness.** Peeking at results, ignoring power, confusing correlation with lift. Design the test before you look at the data.
- **Pretty charts, no insight.** Visualization is argument, not decoration. Every chart needs a title that states the conclusion, not the topic.
- **Can't walk the pipeline end to end.** Knowing the modeling step but not ingestion, validation, or serving. Interviewers probe the seams — own the whole pipeline.
- **Answering before clarifying.** Ambiguous question, instant query. Ask about grain, time window, definitions, and edge cases first — it mirrors the real job.

quiz.q: A redrill plan is effective when it is:
choices: Specific, dated, and tied to named misses from the scored review
quiz.explain: Specificity turns review into training; vague plans evaporate. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: Saying the bug out loud before fixing it is strong because:
choices: It proves you diagnose before patching — and lets the interviewer follow
quiz.explain: Diagnose-then-fix beats flailing; narration turns the fix into evidence of method. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: Narrating during a SQL screen helps because:
choices: The interviewer scores your decomposition and recovery, not just the final query
quiz.explain: Live coding is graded on method; narration exposes the thinking being graded. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: You’re asked about 'Timed mixed-pattern circuits' and your memory blanks. What’s the strongest recovery?
choices: State what you do know precisely, name the boundary, and reason from first principles aloud
Say ‘I don’t know’ and go silent
Change the subject to something you know
quiz.explain: Interviewers score honesty + reasoning: a precise partial answer with clear boundaries beats a confident fabrication every time. Covered in this module's 'Concepts' note.

quiz.q: Mixed-pattern circuits train switching because:
choices: Real screens don't announce the pattern — recognition under time is the tested skill
quiz.explain: Classification speed plus execution: the circuit trains both. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: Saying the bug aloud before fixing it is strong because:
choices: It proves you diagnose before patching — and lets the interviewer follow the fix
quiz.explain: Diagnose-then-fix beats flailing; narration turns the fix into evidence. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: An interviewer hint ('what about the grain here?') should be treated as:
choices: Directional data — restate it and adjust visibly; it's where they want you to go
quiz.explain: Hints mark the path; following them well is part of the score. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: The weak-pattern list's job is to:
choices: Turn each circuit's misses into the next circuit's redrill backlog — training compounds
quiz.explain: The list is the mechanism by which circuits get easier. See the 'Concepts' glossary in this module.

quiz.q: No pausing the circuit clock because:
choices: Pressure management is part of the training stimulus — removing it removes the conversion
quiz.explain: Circuits convert knowledge into performance under pressure. See the 'Hands-on procedure' in this module.

quiz.q: Your readiness report's most important section is:
choices: The remaining costliest pattern with its kill plan — honest about what's left
quiz.explain: Readiness is knowing the gap and the plan, not admiring the strengths. See the 'Project brief' in this module.

scriptLabs.title: Month-over-month revenue growth (SQL)
scriptLabs.brief: The analytics bread-and-butter: aggregate to month grain in a CTE, then LAG for period-over-period growth. Grain first, window second — exactly as the module teaches.
scriptLabs.starter:
-- Columns: month, revenue, prev_revenue, mom_growth_pct
-- Table: orders(order_id, order_date, amount)
SELECT
scriptLabs.hint: Aggregate to month grain first in a CTE, then LAG over the ordered months. Guard division by zero with NULLIF.
scriptLabs.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 2) AS mom_growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

scriptLabs.title: Flag each customer’s latest order (pandas)
scriptLabs.brief: Vectorized groupby-transform: broadcast each customer’s max order date back to every row and compare. No Python loops over rows — the interview bar.
scriptLabs.starter:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'customer_id': [1, 1, 2, 2, 2],
    'order_id':    [11, 12, 21, 22, 23],
    'order_date':  ['2026-01-05', '2026-03-02', '2026-01-01', '2026-02-14', '2026-02-14'],
})

# TODO: add boolean column 'is_latest' — True for each customer's most recent order.
# Vectorized only: no iterrows, no apply over rows.
scriptLabs.hint: Convert to datetime, broadcast the per-customer max with transform, then compare elementwise.
scriptLabs.solution:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'customer_id': [1, 1, 2, 2, 2],
    'order_id':    [11, 12, 21, 22, 23],
    'order_date':  ['2026-01-05', '2026-03-02', '2026-01-01', '2026-02-14', '2026-02-14'],
})

df['order_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['order_date'])
latest = df.groupby('customer_id')['order_date'].transform('max')
df['is_latest'] = df['order_date'] == latest
print(df)

scriptLabs.title: Airflow DAG skeleton
scriptLabs.brief: Write the DAG skeleton you’d defend in a data-engineering interview: schedule, retries with backoff, catchup off, and task dependencies. The orchestration contract in code.
scriptLabs.starter:
# TODO: complete this Airflow DAG 'daily_orders'.
# Requirements: daily schedule, 3 retries with exponential backoff,
# catchup=False, extract >> transform >> load dependencies.
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
scriptLabs.hint: default_args holds retries, retry_delay, and retry_exponential_backoff; dependencies chain with >>.
scriptLabs.solution:
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def extract():
    print("extracting orders since last watermark")

def transform():
    print("cleaning, validating, conforming")

def load():
    print("idempotent upsert into warehouse partition")

with DAG(
    dag_id="daily_orders",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    schedule="@daily",
    catchup=False,
    default_args={
        "retries": 3,
        "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5),
        "retry_exponential_backoff": True,
    },
    tags=["orders", "daily"],
) as dag:
    t_extract = PythonOperator(task_id="extract", python_callable=extract)
    t_transform = PythonOperator(task_id="transform", python_callable=transform)
    t_load = PythonOperator(task_id="load", python_callable=load)
    t_extract >> t_transform >> t_load

scriptLabs.title: Recursive CTE date spine
scriptLabs.brief: Build the complete 2026 calendar as a recursive CTE — the spine you’d left-join sparse facts against so zero-activity days show as zero instead of vanishing.
scriptLabs.starter:
-- TODO: recursive CTE 'spine(d)' with one row per day of 2026.
-- Requirements: anchor row, UNION ALL recursion, termination condition.
SELECT
scriptLabs.hint: Anchor: 2026-01-01. Recursive term: d + INTERVAL '1 day', stopping at 2026-12-31.
scriptLabs.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE spine(d) AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-01-01'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT d + INTERVAL '1 day'
  FROM spine
  WHERE d < DATE '2026-12-31'
)
SELECT d FROM spine;

drills.title: Advanced SQL for Data Engineers
drills.prompt: Putting a filter on an aggregated value in WHERE instead of HAVING is wrong because:
choices: WHERE runs before aggregation — aggregate filters belong in HAVING
drills.explain: Logical query order: WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY aggregates, HAVING filters groups.

drills.title: Statistics and Probability
drills.prompt: A 99%-accurate test for a 0.1%-prevalent disease: most positives are false because:
choices: Base rate: even 1% error on 99.9% healthy people swamps the true positives
drills.explain: Bayes: P(disease|positive) depends on prevalence — rare conditions make false positives dominate.

drills.title: SQL Foundations
drills.prompt: NOT IN is dangerous with NULLs because:
choices: A single NULL in the subquery makes the whole predicate UNKNOWN — zero rows returned
drills.explain: NULL semantics: NOT IN with a NULL never evaluates true; NOT EXISTS doesn’t have this trap.

drills.title: ML Theory
drills.prompt: Deriving on the whiteboard is stronger than reciting because:
choices: It proves understanding — and lets you recover when memory fails mid-step
drills.explain: Derivations are checkable reasoning; recitation is untestable until it breaks.

drills.title: Joins and Subqueries
choices: Assert the merge keys have the expected uniqueness — failing loudly on fan-out
drills.explain: Declaring expected cardinality turns silent row multiplication into a loud error.

drills.title: Advanced SQL for Data Engineers
drills.prompt: A sequential scan in EXPLAIN is a red flag when:
choices: It’s on a large table with a selective filter — a missing or unused index
drills.explain: Full scans are fine for small tables; on large filtered tables they signal missing index support.

drills.title: Statistics and Probability
choices: If the null were true, you’d see results this extreme 3% of the time
drills.explain: It’s a conditional probability under the null — a common misreading is treating it as P(null is true).

drills.title: SQL Foundations
drills.prompt: EXISTS is preferred over IN for ‘has at least one’ because:
choices: It short-circuits on first match and is NULL-safe
drills.explain: Correlated EXISTS stops scanning at the first hit; IN materializes the whole set.

drills.title: ML Theory
drills.prompt: A single decision tree’s boundary is:
choices: Axis-aligned rectangles — splits are one feature at a time
drills.explain: Each split thresholds one feature: the boundary is a union of boxes.

drills.title: Joins and Subqueries
drills.prompt: NOT EXISTS is preferred over NOT IN when:
choices: The subquery column can be NULL — NOT IN then returns nothing
drills.explain: Same NULL trap: NOT EXISTS has clean three-valued-logic semantics.

drills.title: Advanced SQL for Data Engineers
drills.prompt: UNION ALL vs UNION differ in that:
choices: UNION ALL keeps duplicates and skips the dedup sort — faster when dupes are fine
drills.explain: UNION’s implicit DISTINCT costs a sort; ALL avoids it when duplicates don’t matter.

drills.title: Statistics and Probability
choices: The procedure captures the true parameter in ~95% of repeated samples
drills.explain: Frequentist intervals describe the method’s long-run coverage, not a probability about this interval.

drills.title: Top-N per group
drills.prompt: Top 3 salaries per department, keeping ties. Which window function in the filter?
drills.explain: DENSE_RANK keeps ties without gaps: tied 3rd-place rows all survive. RANK would skip numbers; ROW_NUMBER breaks ties arbitrarily.

drills.title: Peeking
drills.prompt: You check your A/B test daily and stop when p < 0.05. The problem:
choices: Peeking inflates the false-positive rate far above 5%
drills.explain: Repeated testing multiplies false-positive chances. Pre-commit sample size or use sequential methods.

drills.title: SCD Type 2
drills.prompt: A customer's address changes and you must preserve history for reporting. Model it with:
choices: New row with effective dates + current flag (Type 2)
drills.explain: Type 2 SCD versions the dimension: each change is a new row, history queryable by date.

drills.title: pandas merge
drills.prompt: df.merge(other, on='id', how='left') unexpectedly doubles rows. Likely cause?
choices: Duplicate keys in `other` — fan-out on merge
drills.explain: Many-to-many key matches multiply rows. Validate key uniqueness (validate='m:1') before merging.

drills.title: Metric choice
drills.prompt: Checkout conversion A/B test: which analysis is most honest?
choices: Effect size with confidence interval, pre-registered metric, run to planned sample
drills.explain: Pre-registration + full run + CIs: the peeking/multiplicity-safe package interviewers want to hear.

scenarios.title: SQL live-coding: top-N per group
scenarios.context: ‘For each department, show the top 3 earners.’ The interviewer is watching you think.

steps.prompt: Before writing anything, what do you clarify?

options.text: The grain and edge cases: one row per what, how to break salary ties, what ‘top’ means
options.why: Grain and tie-breaking decide between ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK — clarifying first picks the right tool.

options.text: Nothing — the question is clear enough
options.why: ‘Top 3’ with ties is genuinely ambiguous; assuming wastes the attempt when the interviewer meant distinct values.

options.text: Which SQL dialect the company uses
options.why: Dialect trivia can wait; the logic is dialect-independent and that’s what’s graded.

options.text: Whether you can use the internet
options.why: Live rounds test unaided reasoning; asking signals you can’t produce the pattern cold.

steps.prompt: Mid-query you blank on the window syntax. Strongest recovery?

options.text: Decompose aloud: ‘I need ranking inside each department — that’s ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) in a CTE, then filter rn <= 3 outside’
options.why: Decomposing into named steps and narrating the pattern shows the interviewer your reasoning even while the exact syntax returns.

options.text: Go silent until the syntax comes back
options.why: Silence is unscoreable; narrated decomposition is gradable and often jogs the memory.

options.text: Write a correlated subquery instead without saying why
options.why: Switching approaches silently looks like flailing; if you pivot, narrate the pivot.

options.text: Say ‘I don’t remember window functions’ and stop
options.why: Surrendering forfeits partial credit; the pattern’s logic is recoverable from first principles.

steps.prompt: The query runs. How do you verify it before declaring done?

options.text: Trace a tiny mental dataset through it: two departments, a tie, and check the output rows by hand
options.why: Mental-dataset verification catches grain, tie, and filter bugs — it’s the live-round equivalent of a test.

options.text: Declare victory — it parsed, so it’s right
options.why: Parsing isn’t correctness; untested SQL in an interview is a guess.

options.text: Ask the interviewer if it’s correct
options.why: Outsourcing verification forfeits the senior signal — checking your own work is the job.

options.text: Add more columns to look thorough
options.why: Extra output doesn’t verify correctness; it just adds surface for new bugs.

scenarios.title: Case round: conversion dropped 10%
scenarios.context: ‘Checkout conversion fell 10% week over week. Diagnose it.’ Whiteboard, 30 minutes.

options.text: Verify the data: instrumentation changes, pipeline delays, definition changes — rule out measurement artifacts
options.why: A large share of ‘metric moves’ are measurement artifacts; theorizing before verifying wastes the round.

options.text: Blame the latest product release
options.why: The newest change is a hypothesis, not a conclusion — and it skips the data-quality check entirely.

options.text: Propose three product hypotheses immediately
options.why: Hypotheses before verification build on possibly-broken data; order matters and it’s graded.

options.text: Ask for a month of raw data to explore
options.why: Boiling the ocean burns the clock; structured diagnosis beats undirected exploration.

steps.prompt: Data checks out — the drop is real. Next?

options.text: Segment: which slice moved (device, channel, cohort, geography)? Then rank hypotheses per segment
options.why: Segmentation localizes the cause; hypotheses ranked per segment turn one mystery into testable pieces.

options.text: Compute the overall average again more carefully
options.why: Recomputing the aggregate you already trust adds nothing; the answer is in the segments.

options.text: Recommend reverting the last release
options.why: Recommending action before localizing the cause is guessing with consequences.

options.text: Build a predictive model of conversion
options.why: Modeling before diagnosing answers a different question — and takes far longer than the round allows.

steps.prompt: Mobile web conversion collapsed; desktop is flat. How do you confirm the mechanism?

options.text: Funnel-by-step on mobile web plus the ‘did the denominator change’ check (traffic mix vs true rate drop)
options.why: The diagnostic query set: localize the funnel step, then separate mix effects from real rate changes — the complete analyst move.

options.text: Declare ‘mobile is broken’ and recommend a rewrite
options.why: A segment-level finding isn’t a mechanism; the funnel step and denominator check are still missing.

options.text: Average mobile and desktop together for the report
options.why: Re-aggregating destroys the segmentation insight you just earned.

options.text: Wait for more data next week
options.why: Deferring a diagnosable problem signals you can’t drive to an answer under time pressure.

scenarios.title: Behavioral: ‘Tell me about a failed analysis’
scenarios.context: The data-science behavioral round. They want the failed-analysis story — told with ownership.

steps.prompt: How do you frame the failure?

options.text: Own it early: what you concluded, why it was wrong, and what the miss cost — then the fix
options.why: Early ownership establishes credibility; the story’s value is in what changed, which needs the honest setup.

options.text: Frame it as actually a success — ‘it taught the team a lot’
options.why: Reframing failure as success dodges the question; interviewers asked for a failure.

options.text: Blame the data quality — it wasn’t your fault
options.why: Data problems are the analyst’s jurisdiction; blaming them fails the ownership test.

options.text: Pick a trivial failure with no stakes
options.why: Stakes-free stories reveal nothing about judgment; pick one where the miss mattered.

options.text: A concrete process change: the validation step you added (e.g. always check the denominator, always segment first)
options.why: A specific changed practice — with evidence it caught something later — turns failure into growth.

options.text: ‘I’m more careful now’
options.why: Vague resolutions aren’t resolutions; interviewers score the mechanism, not the sentiment.

options.text: Nothing — it was a one-off
options.why: ‘One-off’ claims end the learning arc; every real miss has a systemic lesson.

options.text: You switched teams
options.why: Changing scenery isn’t a lesson; it reads as avoidance.

options.text: The lesson as practice: ‘that miss is why I now verify data quality before theorizing — it’s caught two artifacts since’
options.why: A lesson with evidence it stuck is the strongest possible close for a failure story.

options.text: Apologize for the failure again
options.why: Repeated apologies re-center shame instead of growth; one ownership statement suffices.

options.text: Emphasize how bad you felt
options.why: Feelings aren’t the deliverable; the changed practice is.

options.text: Pivot to a success story
options.why: Pivoting away signals discomfort with the failure — land the lesson instead.

trainers.title: SQL pattern trainer
trainers.brief: Rapid-fire SQL interview patterns for the data tracks: joins, window functions, CTEs, and analytics patterns — pick the right clause shape under time pressure, then write the query.

trainers.title: Pipeline design trainer
trainers.brief: Whiteboard-style pipeline design reps: batch vs streaming tradeoffs, backfill safety, idempotency, and DQ gates — structured decision drills for system-design rounds.

choices: Some rows have NULL email — COUNT(column) skips NULLs
mockTasks.explain: COUNT(column) excludes NULLs; COUNT(*) counts every row regardless.

mockTasks.q: Diverging loss (NaN/inf) in training most likely means:
choices: Learning rate too large for the loss curvature
mockTasks.explain: Overshooting the minimum repeatedly: reduce lr (or add scheduling/clipping) first.

mockTasks.q: COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) vs COUNT(*) differ when:
choices: Rows aren’t unique per customer — COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(DISTINCT) counts customers
mockTasks.explain: Grain discipline: know what one row represents before choosing the aggregate.

choices: Using normal-based confidence intervals on sample means from non-normal data (with enough samples)
mockTasks.explain: Sample means converge to normal as n grows — the foundation of classical inference on means.

choices: HAVING — it filters groups after aggregation
mockTasks.explain: WHERE filters rows pre-aggregation; HAVING filters the grouped results.

mockTasks.q: Minimizing MSE is equivalent to MLE under:
mockTasks.explain: The Gaussian likelihood’s log is the squared error (up to constants) — same optimum.

mockTasks.q: Pure transform functions are testable because:
choices: Determinism: no mocks needed, every case is an input/output pair
mockTasks.explain: Purity removes the test setup tax; the function’s contract is its signature.

choices: That the notebook has no hidden out-of-order state — true top-to-bottom reproducibility
mockTasks.explain: Out-of-order execution hides state dependencies; a clean rerun proves the narrative is real.

mockTasks.q: The clearest signal to move from spreadsheet to SQL/Python is:
choices: Manual steps that must be repeated reliably — reproducibility and scale
mockTasks.explain: Repetition + scale + auditability: the point where manual stops being trustworthy.

mockTasks.q: Training loss falling while validation loss rises means:
choices: Overfitting — the model memorizes training noise
mockTasks.explain: The divergence point is where generalization ends; early stopping lives there.

mockTasks.q: Window functions can’t appear in WHERE because:
choices: They’re evaluated after WHERE in the logical query order — filter in an outer query
mockTasks.explain: Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → … → window functions → ORDER BY. Filter one level out.

mockTasks.q: df['x'].apply(f) vs a vectorized equivalent: the difference is:
choices: apply still loops in Python; vectorized ops execute in compiled C — often 10-100x faster
mockTasks.explain: apply is a disguised Python loop; true vectorization pushes the loop into C.

mockTasks.q: Building features before the train/test split risks:
choices: Leakage — statistics from the test set contaminating training features
mockTasks.explain: Any transform that learns from data must be fit on train only, or evaluation is fiction.

mockTasks.q: Formula-based cleaning beats manual edits because:
choices: It’s auditable and re-runnable — manual edits can’t be verified or repeated
mockTasks.explain: Repeatability is the difference between analysis and anecdote.

choices: Randomly zeroes activations so the network can’t rely on any single unit — an implicit ensemble
mockTasks.explain: Forcing redundancy across units prevents co-adaptation; at inference the full network is used (scaled).

mockTasks.q: ‘Each sale alongside its region’s total’ needs:
choices: A window: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region) — detail preserved
mockTasks.explain: Windows add group context without collapsing: every row keeps its identity.

blocks.body: **ROW_NUMBER()**: unique 1,2,3. **RANK()**: 1,2,2,4 (gaps). **DENSE_RANK()**: 1,2,2,3 (no gaps). ‘Top 3 distinct’ → DENSE_RANK; ‘exactly 3 rows’ → ROW_NUMBER.
**LAG/LEAD(col) OVER (ORDER BY t)**: previous/next row — period-over-period. **FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE**: frame edges.
Running total: `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)`. **ROWS** = physical rows; **RANGE** = peer values.
CTE: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY m DESC) AS rn` → outer query `WHERE rn <= N`. Windows can’t go in WHERE — filter one level out.
Randomization unit → primary metric + guardrails → MDE from business value → sample size & runtime from power (80%) → **pre-registered analysis plan**.

**Peeking**: every look compounds false positives — pre-commit the runtime. **Multiple testing**: more metrics, more false wins — correct or prioritize. **Ignoring SUTVA**: network effects break randomization.
CI around the estimate (not just the point), guardrails checked, segment heterogeneity examined. A win with regressed guardrails is a tradeoff, not a victory.
Can’t randomize cleanly, tiny samples, months-long effects, unethical, or obvious from data — then quasi-experiments or ship-with-monitoring.
`groupby(...).agg(...)` for summaries; `.transform(...)` to broadcast back to rows (same shape out); `.filter(...)` on group properties.
Check key uniqueness first; `validate='m:1'` fails loudly on fan-out. `indicator=True` shows merge provenance.
Boolean masks, `np.where`, string methods — never `iterrows`. 10–100x faster and shorter. `apply` is a disguised Python loop.
`chunksize` + incremental aggregation, `usecols`, dtype downcasting. Never assume the data fits in memory.
`pd.to_datetime`, timezone-aware, store UTC. DST makes naive arithmetic ambiguous.
Full vs incremental (watermark: updated_at/CDC). Incremental needs late-arrival handling — it’s an optimization with a correctness contract.
DAGs as code, sensors for external state, retries with backoff for transient failure, SLA + alerting for the on-call reality.
**Idempotent** stages (reruns safe) · partition-scoped backfills · DQ gates at layer boundaries (freshness, volume, schema, distribution) · fail or quarantine, never silently pass bad data.
Grain first, then star schema; SCD Type 2 when history matters; bronze → silver → gold with contracts between layers; dbt tests on every model.

blocks.code:
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)
LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)
SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY dt ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

blocks.body: ROW_NUMBER() in a subquery + WHERE rn <= N. DENSE_RANK keeps ties; ROW_NUMBER never ties.
Subtract ROW_NUMBER() from the date to find contiguous ranges — the classic 'consecutive login days' pattern.
Conditional aggregation: SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END). Portable across dialects.
EXPLAIN the plan: seq scan vs index, nested loop vs hash join, sort spills. 'It depends on the data distribution' is an acceptable start, then reason.
CDC/snapshot → validate → dbt transform → warehouse → DQ tests → marts. Idempotent, backfillable, SLA'd.
Kafka → Flink/Spark → sink. Exactly-once = idempotent sink + transactional offsets. Watermarks handle late data.
Same input → same output on rerun. Merge/upsert keys, not append-only hope.
Freshness, row counts, null rates, distribution checks. Great Expectations / dbt tests in the pipeline, not after.

cheatSheets.title: Stats & A/B testing — the honesty kit

blocks.body: Normal (CLT-backed), binomial (counts), Poisson (rates). Know when each applies.
H0 vs H1, p-value = P(data|H0), α = 0.05 convention. p-hacking = testing until green.
Power analysis → MDE → sample size → randomize → run to completion (no peeking) → analyze with CIs, not just p-values.
Checking early inflates false positives; testing 20 metrics guarantees a 'winner'. Pre-register metrics; correct (Bonferroni/Holm) or sequential methods.
P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). Base rates dominate rare-event inference.
Star: denormalized dims, fewer joins, BI-fast. Snowflake: normalized, storage-efficient, join-heavy. Grain: one row = one fact.
New row per change with effective dates + current flag. History preserved; queries filter on current.
SQL transforms as code: models, tests, docs, lineage. Staging → intermediate → marts.
Insight → evidence → implication → recommendation. One message per chart. Business judgment is the scored skill.

answerBank.q: Window functions vs GROUP BY — when do you use each?
answerBank.a: GROUP BY collapses rows to one per group — use it for pure aggregates. Window functions compute across rows while keeping every row — ‘each employee alongside their department average’ needs AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY dept). The rule: if the question wants detail plus context, it’s a window; if it wants one row per group, it’s GROUP BY.

answerBank.q: How do you design an A/B test?
answerBank.a: Randomization unit, primary metric plus guardrail metrics, MDE from business value, sample size and runtime from a power calculation — and a pre-registered analysis plan before the first user is enrolled. During the run: no peeking (pre-commit the stopping rule), and at read-out I check the confidence interval, guardrails, and segment heterogeneity, not just the point estimate.

answerBank.q: The metric moved — walk me through your diagnosis.
answerBank.a: First, verify the data: instrumentation changes, pipeline delays, definition changes — rule out measurement artifacts. Then segment to find which slice moved, form ranked hypotheses per segment, and test with the diagnostic query set: funnel by segment, cohort check, and the ‘did the denominator change’ query. Only then do I recommend. Data-quality before storytelling — the order is what’s graded.

answerBank.q: Batch vs streaming — how do you choose?
answerBank.a: By latency need versus cost and complexity: batch is simpler, cheaper, and easier to get exactly right — the default. Streaming earns its keep when decisions need minutes, not hours. I name the costs honestly: watermarks and late data, exactly-once complexity, and operational burden. Kappa (one streaming pipeline with log replay) unless I can name why batch is required.

answerBank.q: How do you handle training/serving skew?
answerBank.a: Skew means features at serving time differ systematically from training — usually different code paths computing them. Prevention: shared feature logic via a feature store, point-in-time correctness for training data. Detection: log serving features and monitor input/prediction distributions against the training baseline, with retraining triggers on drift. Same model, different data is a silent failure — so I make the data pipeline the tested contract.

Every model balances two errors: bias is the model being too simple to capture reality (underfitting — consistently wrong), variance is it being too sensitive to the specific data it saw (overfitting — great on past data, bad on new). More data tames variance; the right model complexity tames bias. We pick the sweet spot with validation — testing on data the model hasn’t seen.

answerBank.q: Tell me about a failed analysis.
answerBank.a: STAR with ownership: what I concluded, why it was wrong, and what the miss cost — stated early and plainly. Then the concrete process change it produced (e.g. always verifying data quality before theorizing, always checking the denominator), with evidence the change caught something later. The failure is the setup; the changed practice with proof is the point.

glossary.definition: What one row means (one order-line, one session). The foundation of correct aggregation.
Row multiplication from one-to-many joins — the silent SUM-inflator.
WITH-clause named subquery: readable, testable SQL structure.
Row-preserving analytics: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG/LEAD, running aggregates.
Finding contiguous ranges in sequences (login streaks) via date − row_number grouping.
Rerunnable pipelines producing identical results — merge keys, not blind appends.
Streaming threshold for how late data may arrive before being considered too late.
Central fact table + denormalized dimensions: the BI query pattern.
Slowly Changing Dimension: Type 1 overwrite, Type 2 versioned history, Type 3 limited history.
SQL-first transformation with tests/docs/lineage: the modern T in ELT.
Probability of detecting a real effect (1 − β); set by sample size and MDE.
Minimum Detectable Effect: the smallest lift worth detecting — drives sample size.
Checking results early and stopping at significance: inflates false positives.
Range of plausible effect sizes; more informative than a bare p-value.
Python's DataFrame library: groupby, merges, reshaping — the analysis workhorse.

faq.q: Window functions vs GROUP BY — when?
faq.a: GROUP BY collapses rows; window functions compute across rows while keeping them. Top-N per group, running totals, period-over-period: windows. Simple totals: GROUP BY.

faq.q: How do I talk about query performance in interviews?
faq.a: Read EXPLAIN: join order, access methods, sort spills. Then reason about data distribution and indexes — interviewers want the reasoning, not memorized hints.

faq.q: Batch or streaming for the pipeline design question?
faq.a: Ask about latency requirements first. Then present both with tradeoffs: batch = simpler/cheaper; streaming = complex/costly. Choosing with reasons scores more than picking one.

faq.q: What's the single most common A/B testing mistake?
faq.a: Peeking — stopping early at significance. Pre-register the metric and sample size, run to completion, report CIs.

faq.q: pandas or SQL for the analysis portion?
faq.a: Both appear. SQL for set operations at scale; pandas for exploration and features. The course drills the handoff between them.

faq.q: How deep does the ML portion go?
faq.a: Interview depth: framing, leakage, metrics, overfitting, and ML system design — not research. Enough to survive 'design a churn model' end to end.

faq.q: Star or snowflake — is there a right answer?
faq.a: Star for BI query speed, snowflake for normalized storage — defend with the access pattern. Then discuss SCD handling and grain, which is where the real points are.
